speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today marks the third anniversary of the sinking of the Ocean Ranger. This tragedy, which occurred on February 15, 1982, shocked our nation and brought great grief to the people of Canada, and more directly to the families of the 84 men lost at sea. The suffering of the relatives and friends of the dead, and the continuing trauma of the survivors, bring to mind the price paid by working people.
It is worth remembering, especially during the afterglow of the recently signed Atlantic Accord, that the lives of our workers must be considered before we rush into any activity. The health and safety of the riggers and seamen are as much the responsibility of our Government as the negotiating of transfer payments and energy revenues.
Let us remember the 84 men who lost their lives on February 15, 1982, when we rise to discuss labour code amendments and changes to our legislation. It is through our actions in the House and actions by the Government that future tragedies such as the Ocean Ranger can be avoided.

Mr. Speaker, at 1:30 a.m. on December 15, 1964, with 163 in favour and 78 against, Canada was given its own distinctive flag. We owe this to the courage and determination of a great Canadian, the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson, Leader of the Liberal Party and Prime Minister of Canada from 1963 to 1968.
On February 15, 1965, twenty years ago today-
Order, I am prepared to let the Member finish his statement. I am not prepared to allow displays in the House of Commons because it is against the rules.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: You have a flag.
I am not prepared to allow the displays. I apologize. It is against the rules. I am prepared to let the Member finish his statement.

You will understand why I am so proud, Mr. Speaker.

On February 15, 1965, twenty years ago today, this symbol of Canadian unity and pride was raised above all federal buildings and property, and elsewhere across Canada. The resistance of certain politicians was swept away by the enthusiasm of Canadians for their own distinctive flag.
In fact, Mr. Maxime Guitard, one of the clerks at the Table who was committee clerk at the time, could give us the exact details of this story. Nine Members sitting in the House of Commons at the time are still sitting in the House today.
I take particular pride in recalling this event because it was the most important day in my twenty-one years in politics. Five of the nine who voted in favour were Liberals, and they were Mr. Turner (Vancouver Quadra), Mr. Gray (Windsor-West) and Mr. Chretien, and my good friend Ms. Pauline Jewett, who was a Liberal at the time, and myself. Four of the nine who are still sitting today voted against and belong to the Progressive Conservative Party. They included, I am sorry to say, the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Nielsen).
For us, Mr. Speaker, as it is for all Canadians, for our young people and for all new Canadians, this is one of the most memorable days of our lives.

Mr. Speaker, the arts community and our cultural organizations have been forced to concentrate their efforts on defending themselves against the Government's budget-cutting attacks. As a result, they have not had a chance to develop proposals for improving cultural life in Canada.

February 15, 1985

Major problems remain in addition to those caused by the cut-backs, Mr. Speaker. There are problems of distribution and access to cultural products and to performances. There are particular problems with regard to films, books, magazines, and theatrical performances. Distribution systems must be improved. Governments now subsidize the production of many products and performances that do not get to be seen by many Canadians. These subsidies would not have to be as important numerically if there were more purchases. In short, Governments ought to be purchasing books and magazines for schools, libraries, and other institutions. Such a measure would require federal and provincial co-operation.
We will be having a meeting of federal and provincial Ministers of Culture. I hope that the Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) will bring forward imaginative proposals to improve access to cultural products and performances in Canada, and will discuss these things with his provincial counterparts. More money is needed in this area, but certainly it is important-
I regret to advise the Member that her time has expired.

Mr. Speaker, my constituents of Montmorency-Orleans and their fellow Quebecers are delighted to see the climate of confidence that now reigns in negotiations between the Canadian Government and the Government of Quebec. This is very much to the liking of many Quebecers, at a time when a federal-provincial conference is being held in Regina.
The Canada-Quebec agreements signed to date are impressive both in number and in scope. On December 14 last year, the federal Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) and the Quebec Minister of Intergovernmental Affairs signed the new economic and regional development agreement. Under this agreement, the federal Government will be contributing $1 billion over the next five years.
On January 22, the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) announced the introduction of a program for technological innovation assistance in Quebec, also spread over five years. On February 1, the federal Minister of Communications (Mr. Masse) and the Quebec Minister of Communications concluded an agreement aiming at promoting the development of the communications industry in Quebec.
Finally, the Government of Canada and the Government of Quebec will be spending $100 million on the tourist industry within the next few years.
Mr. Speaker, I could go on in this vein, but I would prefer to emphasize the incredible improvement in Canada-Quebec relations since the present Government came to power and decided to promote the interests of Quebec.

subsubtopic: FUNDING OF UNITED NATIVE NATIONS ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Native Nations represents non status Indians and some off-reserve Indians in British Columbia. Last year the Secretary of State cut their core funding in order to provide funding for the Louis Riel Metis Association of B.C. The Metis Association certainly required the funding, but it should not have been taken from the United Native Nations. This kind of government action makes it very difficult for different aboriginal peoples to achieve unity.
In a similar manner, United Native Nations applied for Indian Affairs funding to hold workshops on proposed changes to the Indian Act which would affect their membership. However, all available funding went to the B.C. Indian Homemakers Association. The homemakers needed this funding and are holding workshops throughout the province. But again we must ask why one legitimate organization was funded at the expense of another equally legitimate organization.
British Columbia Metis and non status people favour the one window concept for Canada employment programs. The single project officer cuts down on red tape and makes it easier for native people to gain access. But they feel that they are not adequately represented on district advisory boards and as a result do not get approval for a fair share of their projects.
I call on the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean), the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie), and the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Miss MacDonald), to look into these concerns and ensure that non status people are not subject to double discrimination.

Mr. Speaker, on February 7, 1985, the Minister of Justice and Attorney General (Mr. Crosbie) announced the establishment of a commission of inquiry on war criminals to be conducted by Mr. Justice Jules Deschenes of the Superior Court of Quebec.
I commend the Government on its efforts to take all responsible steps to ensure any war criminals in Canada are brought
February 15, 1985

to justice, whatever their racial origin. However, Mr. Speaker, we must ensure that while we are seeking out those who have perpetrated crimes against humanity we do not allow such action to reflect poorly on entire ethnic groups. Canada is a society rich in the wealth of ethnic diversity and has benefited enormously from the contribution of our citizens who have emigrated to Canada and raised their families here.
One such ethnic group with which I am familiar is the Ukrainian Canadian community of some 600,000 people, 90 per cent of whom are Canadian born. Many of these Ukrainian Canadians, indeed, fought in the Canadian Armed Forces during the Second World War against the Nazis. Some of them fought in their country to liberate it from Russian and Nazi oppression.
Should individuals of a particular ethnic group be accused of atrocities, it is imperative that the group as a whole not be treated in a manner which ignores its vital involvement in and contribution to Canada.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we Canadians need to be reminded that on February 16, 1918, Lithuania was restored to independence and flourished as a free democratic state for 20 years, along with its neighbours Latvia and Estonia.
In June, 1940, all three were subjugated once again when the Soviet Union signed the Ribbentrop-Molotov Non-Aggression Pact, and marched in and annexed them.
We take for granted the freedoms that the Lithuanian people are denied, but they are still continuing the struggle for liberation. The refusal of Canada to recognize de jure the incorporation of Lithuania into the Soviet Union, and the welcome of the consuls of the Governments in exile of the Baltic states, constitute important acts which help to keep alive the hopes and aspirations of these valiant peoples, many of whose citizens are now our fellow Canadians.
I would ask that Members of the House associate themselves with these sentiments on this sixty-seventh anniversary, so that these courageous peoples know that we have not forgotten them.

subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS-ALLEGED REQUEST BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Over the past several weeks we have directed several questions to the Minister concerning United States' plans for nuclear deployment in this country, and have always received assurances that Canada would exercise its independent decision and not receive such weapons.
We now have reports that the United States State Department has sent communiques to the Government insisting that Canada must accept nuclear weapons on our soil. This not only contradicts the Minister's own statements but is a clear case of nuclear colonialism. We would like to know what in fact is in that telegram and, more particularly, when did the Minister receive it? Finally, will the Minister today issue a statement totally rejecting the American request and saying that it is outrageous that they should suggest anything to an independent country?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS-ALLEGED REQUEST BY UNITED STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as is usually the case in my responses to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, I would say that his facts are completely wrong. There was no such request by the Government of the United States to the Government of Canada. There was, so far as I know, no suggestion by the Government of the United States to anyone that Canada should accept nuclear arms. There was, so far as I know, an instruction by the Department of State of the United States to their ambassador here in Ottawa to be in touch with us
February 15, 1985

expressing concern about the degree to which countries with which the United States has treaty arrangements were going to honour those arrangements.
The question of nuclear arms on Canadian soil did not arise, because the position of the Government of Canada on the question of nuclear arms on Canadian soil is abundantly clear. We do not allow nuclear arms to be stationed on Canadian soil. In the event of any contingency plan which might call for the stationing of nuclear arms here, this Government retains its right to refuse nuclear arms on Canadian soil, and this Government would be prepared to exercise our option to refuse nuclear arms on Canadian soil if we believed that to be in the interests of Canada.

subsubtopic: DEPLOYMENT OF WEAPONS-ALLEGED REQUEST BY UNITED STATES
speechtext: Order, with great respect to the Minister.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the same Minister. We have already seen how the United States has taken retaliatory action against New Zealand over the rejection of the placement of naval bases in that country.
Placement!
The visit of naval forces.
Oh, oh!
Are Members opposite interested in the sovereignty of this country or not? Do they want to hear the question?
We are interested in the facts.

We would like to know exactly what communication was issued by the U.S. ambassador to this country. Also, is it not time that this country took the initiative and asked for a full ministerial meeting of NATO Ministers to discuss how and in which ways all those countries which are allies of the United States would participate in both the planning and development of that deployment strategy, so that we would be assured that we have the independence and sovereignty to make that decision, and not have it imposed upon us, as the report now says it must?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have told the Hon. Member and the House on several occasions that we are looking at ways in which we can expand the parameters of definition of emergency so that there might be a greater opportunity for countries that are involved to have more lead time in making decisions. I repeat the point that this country, under this Government, would retain the right to refuse nuclear weapons on Canadian soil.
Let me come to Canadian sovereignty. This Government actively defends Canadian sovereignty. That is why, as I said yesterday in committee, this Government wants to proceed
Oral Questions
with the north warning system which will protect and assert Canadian sovereignty, whereas the Hon. Member in his questions as recently as yesterday indicates that he wants to leave open gaps in the radar warning system now, gaps which threaten Canadian sovereignty and threaten Canadian security.

Mr. Speaker, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs knows, there is a report today in The New York Times which says that indeed an agreement exists between the Government of Canada and the Government of the United States, and it would permit the locating of nuclear weaponry in Canada under certain circumstances. I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether there is such an agreement in existence between Canada and the United States. If so, does that agreement contain the veto right of Canada, that is, the right to say no? Third, since the right to say no would also entail the right to say yes, will the Minister use the occasion to convey to the United States that, under no circumstances, will we permit the locating of nuclear weaponry on Canadian soil?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will deal with those matters in order. There is no such agreement. Second, there is, as the Hon. Member probably knows, a NATO decision from the NATO summit meeting in December, 1957, when it was decided that NATO should establish stocks of nuclear weapons which would be available to the alliance in case of emergency. Heads of government agreed in 1957, it stands, and I quote:
The deployment of these stocks and missiles and arrangements for their use, will accordingly be decided in conformity with NATO defence plans and in agreement with the states directly concerned.
That is paragraph 21 of the Paris heads of government communique. That is the authority on which I have been answering questions. That is the authority on which I have said, and repeat categorically now, that this country retains the right to refuse nuclear weapons on Canadian soil in any emergency.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with care to what the Minister had to say. He did not reply to the crucial third part of that question. Since the right to say no also logically entails the possibility of saying yes, and since Canadians have made it abundantly clear in every part of this land that under no circumstances do we want nuclear weaponry located, deployed, parked, or in any way put on Canadian soil, will the Minister now make it clear to the people of Canada, and soon to the United States, that under no circumstances will we accept nuclear weapons in Canada?

February 15, 1985
Oral Questions

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member, who follows these questions carefully, takes them seriously, and does not try to mislead Canadians about their implications, will know that there have been discussions in the House for some time on the so-called contingency plan in the United States. There are no such plans now. In the event that contingency plans were developed, the contingency of which they would take account would be a circumstance to attack. In that circumstance, Canada has the right to say yes or no to nuclear arms. I am not in a position at this time to be able to say how we would respond, not knowing the conditions of attack that might prevail.
The Hon. Member will understand the conditions of attack, which we all devoutly hope will never occur, are conditions which are almost impossible for any of us to conceive in detail in advance. I do say to him that this Government retains, and so long as I am here the Government would exercise, the right to say no to nuclear arms, even in those circumstances, if we believe that to be in the Canadian interest, and it would be Canadians, not anyone else, who would make that decision of Canadian interest.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, the use of nuclear weaponry at any point, according to all the literature that I have read and I imagine the Minister has read, would be an act of complete and utter folly. If one agrees with that as the premise, will the Minister agree that what follows from that is that no circumstance, a real emergency, an alleged emergency, or any other circumstance down the road, should lead us to the conclusion that we could ever accept nuclear weapons, because the use of them under any circumstances will mean mutual suicide involving the United States and the Soviet Union? If that should happen, so far as it is possible, we do not want to be any part of that process. Therefore, will he now say that under no circumstances will we have nuclear weapons in Canada?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I agree that nuclear conflict would be folly for the world. I believe that everyone in the House shares the view that it would be folly for the world. I think we all hope that that folly will never arise. Indeed, one of the reasons why this Government is pursuing as vigorously as it is the establishment of the northern warning system, and the modernization of our radar system, is that that is a part of the deterrence system which for so long has prevented that folly from occurring.
What the Hon. Member is asking me to do is to predict how we would act in the event of an attack which all of us hope does not occur. It is impossible to give that answer before those circumstances, which we hope never arise, do arise.
I repeat my assurance. The Government of Canada has insisted on retaining in Canadian hands the right to make the decision on how we would react even in that most extreme of circumstances. Even at that height of folly, it will be a Canadian decision and not a decision of anyone else.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister of Finance. The First Ministers' love-in threatened to turn sour yesterday when the Premiers attacked rising interest rates. Surely for a Government which prides itself on consultation and consensus making, and which promised lower interest rates in its election platform, that is not the final response. Columbia and Nova Scotia at least. As the Minister knows, today nuclear vessels can enter the harbours of Vancouver, Halifax, and other ports in Canada with live U.S. nuclear weapons on board.

subtopic: UNITED NATIONS EDUCATIONAL, SCIENTIFIC AND CULTURAL ORGANIZATION CANADIAN MEMBERSHIP AND FUNDING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. He will know that the Government of France has just announced an increased contribution to certain of the activities of UNESCO. It is not the intention of the Government of Canada to follow that example.
Earlier this week I had the opportunity to meet with the executive of the Canadian Commission to UNESCO, and at that time I expressed our very grave concern about the state of that organization. I made it clear that our intention was not to make a decision until the meeting in the fall with regard to UNESCO. I also told them that we were not satisfied with the present pace of reform. I indicated that there was an overwhelming concern in Canada for the strength of international institutions and the strength of the United Nations system, and that that was the basis upon which I was urging reform in UNESCO.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Communications, who has instituted a policy review of the CBC. Would he now undertake to make this a public review and allow public hearings on the subject? If not, how many more protests, demonstrations, assemblies, and advertisements in newspapers will it take before he realizes that the Canadian public is extremely dissatisfied with his conduct of the Department and wants some input into the CBC review?

Mr. Speaker, I think the Hon. Member is talking about two
separate issues which she, either for political reasons or out of ignorance, has a tendency to confuse. There are two entirely different problems here.
First of all, we have the statement by the Minister of Finance prescribing budgetary cutbacks in all Government envelopes. As part of these cutbacks, the CBC has been asked to make a contribution that seemed and still does seem to us entirely fair and proportionate.
Second, the Government has made a commitment to review Canada's broadcasting industry, which includes the CBC. This decision was announced last fall, and in the weeks to come we shall be in a position to make a full statement on the mechanisms we intend to introduce to ensure the participation of Canadians in the future of broadcasting in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister began by answering a question which I put to him a couple of weeks ago. I was not asking about cut-backs. I was asking about the policy review and when the Canadian public will be able to have some input into it. Is it normal that the Canadian public has to place advertisements in newspapers to get through to the Minister? He refuses to meet with groups. When will he listen to them? When will he let the public talk about what they want their public broadcasting system to do?

Mr. Speaker, in answer to the first part of the question I said that in due time, that is, within a few weeks, the Government will be announcirig to Canadians and to the House how those who are interested in the future of broadcasting in Canada, and especially that of the CBC, can make their views known within the consultation process.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Minister of Employment and Immigration. In the 1984 Annual Report on Future Immigration Levels the Minister gave top priority to encouraging business immigration to Canada. Given the fact that this kind of immigration benefits our economy immensely because of the jobs it creates, can the Minister tell the House what specific measures have been taken, or will be taken, to encourage and promote entrepreneur immigration to Canada?
February 15, 1985

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Vezina (Minister for External Relations):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the Hon. Member for her question.
I can inform her that we intend to maintain the immigration program for entrepreneurs and that we have given special training to thirty-five visa officers in order to respond more effectively and extend a more cordial invitation to prospective immigrants.
We also have a working group that includes the Employment and Immigration Commission, the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and External Affairs, and whose role is to find effective ways of getting more entrepreneurs to come to this country and give us the benefit of their expertise and talents, in order to generate jobs and improve our quality of life.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. This morning's Globe and Mail detailed the Bata Shoe Company's non-compliance with the voluntary code of conduct for Canadian firms operating in South Africa. They have engaged in union busting, they pay wages 50 per cent below the poverty line, and they have refused to report to the Canadian Government because they say this would offend South African authorities.

Western Grain Stabilization Act Grain Stabilization Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Agriculture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I want to express my appreciation to the House Leader of my Party (Mr. Hnatyshyn) for recognizing the need to proceed on this piece of legislation as soon as possible. I know that my House Leader, my Leader and indeed the entire caucus of our Party recognize the importance of this piece of legislation.
Second, they also recognize that, in order for western farmers to receive benefits as early as possible, it would be necessary for us to take early action on this piece of legislation. This Bill is before the House today as a result of that understanding and appreciation of the difficulties which exist in western Canadian agriculture.
We have sought and received unanimous consent to proceed with Bill C-29 through all stages in the House today. I want to acknowledge that co-operation and the co-operation that has been extended to us by the House Leader of the Official Opposition, the House Leader and agriculture critic for the NDP.
For that reason I hesitate to express my extreme concern about what I just witnessed a few moments ago in the exchange between the Deputy Prime Minister and the official spokesperson for the Official Opposition. His Party is denying us consent to refer to committee three very major tax items which have been made known to us in representations over the years by people in the agriculture industry. They are to study and hopefully act on the issue of capital gains, the problems associated with Section 31, and to further study the issue of agri-bonds. It dumbfounds me to witness this continuing reluctance on behalf of the Official Opposition to give us an opportunity to refer these three items to an appropriate standing committee. These items could then be studied and agricultural organizations in this country could have an opportunity to have the input for which they have been asking for many years.
I think that is a very serious matter. Although I appreciate the co-operation that we have received from both Opposition Parties with respect to this Bill, I could not let this opportunity pass without registering my very deep concern about the continuing reluctance on behalf of the Official Opposition to refer these matters to a standing committee.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of bending the rules or doing anything of that nature. However, offers have been forthcoming from our House Leader. The record from as late as a few moments ago will show that there was no attempt to bend the rules, by any stretch of the imagination. I am sure Canaian farmers will recognize the situation. As of today we, the Government, and the New Democratic Party are prepared to refer these matters to the appropriate standing committee, but the Official Opposition is not prepared as of today to do that.
I do want to make mention of the fact that this Bill would have been introduced and perhaps this speech might well have been made by my colleague, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), but because the First Ministers' conference is still in progress in Regina, Saskatchewan, and the Minister of State for the Wheat Board is attending that conference, I am acting on his behalf on this legislation.
It is with serious concern for western Canada's grain producers that I wish to speak on the proposed amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act. This is a critical time for grain farmers. Thousands of them are caught in a tight cost-price squeeze. It is important that they receive help, and it is important that they receive help as soon as possible. Spring seeding time is less than three months away, and somehow between now and then grain producers have to come up with a lot of cash or credit, enough to buy seed, fertilizer, pesticides, fuel and maybe even machinery. For a lot of producers, that will be difficult. The drought took a large toll among prairie grain crops last summer. In some areas, hail and even flooding reduced crop yields. For many farmers it was the second bad year in a row. According to the most recent Statistics Canada Figures, 1984 wheat production fell by 21 per cent from the previous year. Total grain production in western Canada was down by an estimated 6 per cent from 1983 and 16 per cent from the previous five-year average. On top of that, operating and depreciation charges had increased and are expected to go up again in the coming year.
Planting time is the most expensive time of the year for grain producers. It is estimated that in 1984 prairie grain farmers spent over $1.4 billion on direct crop inputs, seed, fertilizer and pesticides. We can figure that fuel, machinery and labour costs were also in the 10-digit bracket. For 1985, Statistics Canada predicts a slight increase in operating and depreciation charges. Obviously, the capital requirements to plant a new crop are substantial.
On January 11 the Canadian Wheat Board announced that western grain farmers would receive $688 million in final payments for grain they delivered during the 1983-84 crop year. That brings to $5,037 billion the total amount of money they received for grain sold through the Wheat Board last year. While that may sound like a lot a money, I would point out that it is $261 million less than prairie grain producers received through the Wheat Board the year before.
February 15, 1985

The bottom line, Mr. Speaker, is this: with less grain to deliver over the next few months, many western producers will be hard-pressed to meet their interest payments and come up with the cash or credit they need to put this year's crops in the ground. Obviously, our western grain producers need all the help they can get, and they need it soon. That is why I am introducing for second reading Bill C-29, a Bill to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act.
The main intent of this legislation is to amend the Act so that interim payments could be issued during the crop year, and even before spring seeding. Such payments could be authorized as long as they are made without risk of overpayment. I have discussed producers' severe need for cash flow this spring, and the probability of a large pay-out for the 1984-85 crop year. This amendment would allow for a substantial payment to be made early this spring and before seeding.
The second amendment involves a small housekeeping matter. It would retroactively deem all previous Orders in Council raising the maximum level of grain sale proceeds eligible for levy payments under the Act to have been passed, registered and published in the Canada Gazette in accordance with the Statutory Instruments Act. This is a matter which was left outstanding by the previous Government when the Act was amended in 1984.
The Western Grain Stabilization Plan is a voluntary program designed to provide farmers with funds during years of low income. Participating producers currently contribute 1.5 per cent of grain sales to the fund, and the federal Government puts in nearly 3.5 per cent, or roughly $2.30 for every dollar contributed by farmers. Whenever net cash flow falls below the previous five-year average, the fund makes a pay-out.
For the 1983-84 crop year, the Western Grain Stabilization Plan paid out $223 million to prairie farmers, $100 million in August and $123 million in November. Because of amendments to the Act last June, the pay-out was triggered under a new formula for calculating net cash flow on a per tonne basis. I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that it was a welcome payment, but it would have been appreciated even more if it had been in the hands of western farmers earlier. If the amendments that I am proposing today had been in place last spring, the first $100 million of the 1983-84 payment could have been in farmers' hands sooner.
Since its inception in 1976, the Western Grain Stabilization Plan has made pay-outs in 1977, 1978 and 1984. As of this date, an individual farmer contributing at the maximum allowable rate has paid a total of $6,825 in levies and received stabilization payments totalling $10,750. Because of poor prospects for grain farmers in the current year, a substantial pay-out for 1984-85 is projected. This is based largely on the reduced volume of marketings.
Farmers, by the very nature of their business, must take risks. They have to gamble on the weather, the markets, and on interest rates, so most farmers will use every available means to protect their incomes. The Western Grain Stabilization Program is a very worth-while income assurance program,
Western Grain Stabilization Act
and producers have recognized it as such. The number of grain farmers participating in the Western Grain Stabilization Plan has increased, not significantly but it has increased year by year. In 1976, the year the program started, 74 per cent of all grain producers enrolled. Today the program has over 77 per cent enrolment.
For the remainder of this crop year, the outlook for grain sales is not spectacular. Producer marketings of the major grains to date are ahead of marketings for this period last year, but exports are lower due to the decline in production last summer. For the remainder of this crop year and next, exports are expected to remain below the level of the previous two years.
However, we can expect to feel market effects of a 13 per cent increase in 1984-85 in world oilseed production and larger wheat supplies in many countries. The latest estimates indicate a six million to seven million tonne decline in marketings of the seven major grains in 1985. Estimating average receipts at $160 per tonne, that represents a significant shortfall in farm income, even with the $668 million in the 1983-84 final Wheat Board payment.
For these reasons there is a strong possibility that a pay-out will be triggered for the 1984-85 crop year extending from last August 1 to this coming July 31. Knowing that, I believe we have a responsibility to see that it gets into the hands of producers as quickly as possible. No matter how large or how small the payment might be, timing is a crucial factor. It makes a lot of sense to put as much as possible into the hands of producers as early as possible and thereby save them some extra interest rate costs.
Moreover, experience has shown that when farmers have more cash available in the spring, they use higher levels of fertilizers and pesticides and in the end result receive higher yields. As a farmer, as a Member of Parliament and as Minister of Agriculture, I have supported the Western Grain Stabilization Plan. However, I realized from the beginning that it was not sensitive enough to the real cash flow needs of farmers. I have always maintained that the legislation was not flexible enough. That is why last June when the Act was being amended to allow for a one-time only interim payment, I said that the amendments did not go far enough. I complained about the fact that we were not given more time in the standing committee to make more improvements to the Bill. I pointed out that because the legislation was still flawed, indeed it would require further improvements. I stated then, as I have said today, that the Western Grain Stabilization Act should be amended to permit payments in any year that a pay-out is likely to be triggered. Had this matter been dealt with last June, of course this Bill and its amendments would not be necessary now.
On behalf of grain producers in western Canada, I urge all Hon. Members of the House to give their support to Bill C-29. By passing the proposed amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act, we will be assisting a major component at a

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act time when that component certainly is in need of assistance and help. It is a very important component in the total Canadian agricultural industry.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, let me say at the outset to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) that, as we have previously indicated, we are prepared to support this Bill and give it quick dispatch through the House, hopefully within the period allotted to it during this day's sitting. We do so because we recognzie, as does everyone, that there is a serious cash flow problem and that it is important to try to provide a major interim payment. Furthermore, a major plank in our own agricultural program last summer was that we would bring in amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act allowing for interim payments as the first piece of legislation.
I notice that this is not the First piece of legislation the Government has brought in, but it is close enough that we will not quibble over the timing. However, we feel that probably quicker action could have been taken on it in the sense that many farmers, now that we are into the second week of February, have been somewhat confused or uncertain about what their cash flow would be without knowing the direction. Even with the quick and speedy passage of the Bill through the House today, it will take several weeks to work out the formula for the interim payment. Therefore, many farmers will not know what to expect perhaps until early March and, as the Minister of Agriculture knows, that is getting close to seeding time. However, at least Members of Parliament can do their part and give the Bill quick and easy support during this day's debate.
1 wish the Government had been equally as co-operative as we are trying to be in the notice of motion it put forward relating to the reference it wanted to the agricultural committee. It is important to make clear that our objection was not about the reference itself but about the way in which it was done. No notice was put on the Order Paper, no notice of motion whatsoever was provided by the Government House Leader (Mr. Hnatyshyn). Yesterday we were simply presented with a fait accompli, with a request on which we had not been given any notice. Our House Leader was not in the Chamber. We did not have an opportunity to discuss it in caucus or to discuss it with our House Leader, nor did we have an opportunity today to comment upon our problem because we were not recognized.
I want to make it very clear that we are not opposed to the reference itself. We simply suggest that perhaps the Minister of Agriculture could take the matter up with his House Leader and indicate that for future reference it would help if the Government House Leader gave proper notification to the Official Opposition about the Government's intention. Then we would co-operate and respond in like kind.

Mr. Speaker, now that we have somewhat cleared the question of procedure, I will return to the short debate. In endorsing the proposal of the Government to bring about a quick interim payment, I am pleased to note-I believe I can take this meaning from the Minister's words-
February 15, 1985

that the position taken by many Conservative Members of Parliament last year during the course of the debate amending the Western Grain Stabilization Act, that they in fact thought that that Act should be abolished, is no longer the position of that Party. I recall many times during that debate members of that Party bringing forward the case that it was time to abolish the Western Grain Stabilization Act because it was not useful, not effective, had no purpose or support and that it was about time to sit down.
At that time, as Minister responsible in the House of Commons for the Canadian Wheat Board, I was somewhat surprised by those comments. I was particularly surprised because they came from western Members of Parliament from the Provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta. We are pleased to note that at least that particular faction or point of view which was previously expressed has not been accepted by the Government. We would hope that one of the purposes of this amendment is to substantiate the endorsement of the Conservative Government on the value of the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I am pleased to hear the Minister add his own personal words of support. We can now proceed with some assurance in the future that this Act will not be abolished.
The press release put out by the Minister of State responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) indicated that there might be further amendments. Frankly, that gave us some cause for concern. We believe it might reflect the fact that the opinion so loudly and frequently expressed by Conservative Members of Parliament last June will not now be the case.
We all appreciate that the peculiar conditions caused by the weather in western Canada this year will have a serious impact upon western farmers. It is also important to note that there is a continuing concern, particularly in the case of grain farmers, about the problems to be faced this summer, such as locust and insect infestation. I believe it is important at this time for the Government to indicate what contingency plans it may have in response to that.
We have certain mechanisms available such as the Western Grain Stabilization Act. We would obviously like to pursue those. There may be other questions. That is why I want to express one very deep concern on behalf of our Party. There was no mention on the agenda of the First Ministers' conference of agriculture and the problems that it faces. It was particularly ironic that the meeting is being held in Regina, which is the centre of the grain-growing area of western Canada, yet there was nothing on the agenda that would deal specifically with the problems of agriculture, although we know how serious those problems are.
That issue has been somewhat bootlegged into those discussions by the discussion brought forward on interest rates. We all know that is one matter that is affecting the agricultural community severely. During the time that we have in committee, the Minister might avail himself of some opinion as to why, at such an important First Ministers' meeting, agriculture and other productive questions, such as fisheries, were not
Western Grain Stabilization Act on the agenda. There seemed to be an avoidance of dealing with those issues of natural resources and resource production which are so essential to our economy. They received virtually no attention whatsoever.
The lumber, fishing and agriculture industries are areas where there is great concern about international markets, financing, investment and the level of cash flow which those key industries face. We are surprised and we are concerned. We hope there might be an opportunity to discuss this. Perhaps I can make a suggestion. As a follow up to the First Minister's conference, a second similar high-level meeting of First Ministers might be called to deal with questions concerning the resource industries, agriculture, fishing, mining and lumber, the basket of issues dealing with productive renewable resources in this country and how we intend to go about financing them.
1 want to raise another concern and I would welcome very much the response of the Minister. He was not in the House last week when we had an Opposition Day dealing with agricultural problems.
I was here.

I do not think he was here when I spoke. Perhaps he was behind the curtain or on some other major activity. It is not that I necessarily feel that he had to be a party to my eloquence, but there was one important issue that was raised and I have not heard any response from the Canadian Government on this. I refer to the way in which we intend to cope with the very substantial, almost radical change being proposed by the United States in its agricultural programs. As he knows, Secretary of Agriculture Block and the budget proposals by President Reagan propose a major elimination of their subsidy programs. The solution put forward by the United States Secretary of Agriculture-I apologize to the House if this is out of order-is that they will market the hell out of their products in order to keep up the cash flow of U.S. farmers. That represents a very major and serious question. We know the incredible international market power of U.S. commodities. We also know that they can depress a market, bring it down or dominate a market.
If in fact the United States Government is moving toward what might be called even more aggressive marketing strategies than they already have in order to provide compensation for their farmers due to losses in farming subsidies, that obviously puts our own grain business in very serious jeopardy and causes serious potential problems. We now have problems with the European Common Market. There appears to be a major problem looming on the horizon by a change in U.S. policy. That is something that should not be simply left to circumstance or after-the-fact policy. It is something we should be looking at now.
We would encourage and request from the Minister of Agriculture that this Government address its own levels of concerns to the Secretary of Agriculture. I believe he has had meetings with him. We know that there is a summit meeting between the President and the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney)

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act
coming up in March. We hope that will be a matter on that agenda and that we will ensure that any attempts by the United States to change its grain policies and subsidies programs will not work to the detriment of our own grain-marketing position.
We have seen, and the Minister properly drew this to the attention of the House, that the Wheat Board this year has performed in a remarkable fashion, not with great prices but with respectable prices and, more important, is continuing to secure our markets. We also know that there are storm clouds in that respect. The Chinese, for example, for three years have had very successful crops. They have been a major buyer of Canadian grains. I do not think anyone would want to be critical of the achievements of the Chinese in developing major grain production. Changes in their own philosophy are a major reason for that.
It does raise, however, questions about our own marketing strategy and the fact that one of our very good customers may now be reaching a point of self-sufficiency. In fact, it may even become an exporter of grain over the next year or two. That, again, will have a major impact upon the western farmer. It comes back to the point I want to make. We are coming to a crunch point or crisis point in the area of international grain marketing and the need for looking at forms of agreement that may be arrived at.
I would hope, and again this is by way of recommendation, that one of the initiatives of this Government will be a very positive, aggressive attempt to rework and rearrange international grain agreements with our partners. I know it is difficult. I am not downplaying the barriers or handicaps, but it is necessary.
I want to express a note of regret. In reading very carefully the trade paper put forward by the colleague of the Minister of Agriculture, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Kelle-her), there is virtually no mention of commodities. There is virtually no mention of what the trade strategy or policy would be of this Government in relation to those commodity markets. I was surprised at that absence. When you consider the amount of money that the grain trade makes for this country, it should be considered almost number one in the trade strategy; but it was not mentioned at all.
I again urge this Government to provide an addendum or supplementary trade paper, prepared in concert with the Wheat Board and the Department of Agriculture, on a grain trade strategy or commodity trade strategy so that we can have proper consultation and know where we want to go. It is time we looked at the horizon we are facing, at what is happening in the United States and with some of our market partners. We should realize we are into some turbulence in the international market area and, therefore, need a very clear response.
With those questions being raised, all done in a spirit of trying to provide some constructive criticism, we would simply say again to the Minister that we will support this Bill. We hope we can have full passage today and that we can get on
with the business. As I say, we don't mind, when we have a good idea, if the Government copies it.

Mr. Speaker, it is our understanding that the amendments to the Western Grain Stabilization Act will go through all stages here in the House today. I hope that is true because we really want to make it possible for the Government to get the payments out to farmers as early as possible.
First, I would like to congratulate the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer) for having this Bill put before the House, albeit a bit later than he had hoped. I also want to congratulate the Minister on getting the support of Liberal Members for this Bill. Liberal Members would not accept this very amendment as late as June 27, 1984, so I congratulate the Minister on getting the support of members of the Liberal Party for this amendment.
I hope that the Government will be more efficient than the previous administration in getting the money out to the farmers. If this Bill passes and there is a pay-out this year, hopefully the farmers will receive it before seeding because that is one of their major requirements. We all know that and there is no reason why we should spend a great deal of time belabouring it.
I do want to talk about a number of concerns that we in the New Democratic Party have about the whole approach to agriculture and the solutions which exist for its problems. The Minister spent a considerable amount of time listing the woes of the farmers and the problems faced by agriculture. Since he knows and is able to articulate these problems so well, hopefully he is also ready to put before the House what he believes are the solutions. We appreciate the fact that, as far as financing is concerned, the Government has decided to have one of the Standing Committees discuss the tax and financing structure of agriculture. We will co-operate with that because we think that that is one, but only one, of the real problems facing agriculture.
We recognize, like the Government, the provincial Governments and certainly the farmers, that there is a real problem facing agriculture. The problem consists not only of financing but of input costs, interest rates and financing methods. These are things about which we must do something. The farmers, the provincial Governments and the federal Government together will have to take a global look at agriculture to identify the problems and find their solution, and this must be done if farming is to survive.
Members of each of the Parties in this House have committed themselves over and over again to supporting the family farm. However, it is the small family farm that is being devastated by the situation in which agriculture finds itself. We cannot blame this situation on one little factor, like not having stabilization or having high interest rates. We must look at all of these factors. I think it is time the Government, the provincial Governments, farm groups and the farmers take
February 15, 1985

a look at the global problems of agriculture and try to come up with some solutions.
There are a number of small solutions to be found. There is stabilization for a number of products and there is supply management for some of the commodities that we sell in the market. There are marketing boards which operate very effectively. As well, there are insurance plans that cover portions of the structure of agriculture but we still find ourselves in the position of having a large number of farms going under. However, we must begin looking at agriculture globally and making all of the decisions for change in the light of the projects and the marketing and stabilization plans that are presently in place. Let us look at agriculture globally to see if there is not something that can be done.
We all recognize, of course, that the obvious and very simple answer to the problems of agriculture is to pay for the commodity what it costs the farmer to produce it. That is a very simple and easy answer but one which is a little more difficult than that to put into place since we do exist within a world market. However, that solution is one at which we should look. Simple as it seems, we have over the years been unable to grapple with that particular approach. Therefore, we must look at it again.
We have needed to implement these many plans because the approach of the previous Government and of many of the provincial Governments has been do deal with a problem when it arises rather than to take a look at the reasons for the problem. Insurance plans or stabilization plans have been put into place so that apple producers and cheese producers could survive for one more year. That is exactly what we are doing by putting this particular plan in place.
We are hoping that the Western Grain Stabilization Plan will help the grain farmers or some of them survive for one more year. I think we are kidding ourselves by believing that this kind of solution will be the only solution. As much as we appreciate the fact that this is one method of getting money into the hands of grain farmers right now, it will not solve the problems of agriculture.
Since it is unlikely that the Government will come up with a global solution, one which would put in place the kind of income security to which we think farmers are entitled, we are now dealing only with the problems of grain farmers in particular. For a considerable amount of time, members of the New Democratic Party have been proposing to amalgamate the insurance plan for grain that we have in western Canada with the Grain Stabilization Plan. This particular approach has been put before the Government of Canada by several groups throughout the country. The Canada grains group, a branch of the Minister's own Department, has on a number of occasions made representations suggesting that we should amalgamate insurance with stabilization so that all grain growers or those who wish to participate can insure themselves against both the market and the weather. It would be a voluntary and contributory plan which would be actuarially sound. The grain growers, the federal Government and the provincial Governments would contribute.
Western Grain Stabilization Act If I could call it one o'clock, I will continue after the lunch recess.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the House rose at one o'clock, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) had the floor.

Mr. Speaker, when we broke for lunch I was discussing the possibility of amalgamating the existing insurance plan in western Canada with the Western Grain Stabilization Plan in order to have an over-all plan which would be much more effective and valuable. The existing insurance plan provides a structure which covers most of the Prairies. The provincial Governments provide the administration, the federal Government provides a portion of the funds and the farmers also make a contribution to the plan. If that approach were tailored to the needs of every farmer, they would be better off in the end. It would allow the stabilization plan to be tailored for each farmer, region and crop. If the Government intends to amend the Act later in the year to look at this type of approach, we would be happy to exchange a more comprehensive plan for the present Western Grain Stabilization Plan.
I do not think the Government has made a commitment, nor do I think it is prepared to make the kind of commitment, which would provide income security to grain farmers. However, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board indicated an interest in having a full review of the Act. We would commend that action. There are a number of areas in the Act which need to be reviewed.
When the Act was passed in 1978, a number of Members in the House suggested that certain amendments should be made. Since that time the Act has been amended several times and members of the NDP have reiterated the fact that there are weaknesses in the Act which should be corrected. We would congratulate the Minister if it is his intention to amend the Act. We hope that it is done very quickly. After this amendment is passed and the pay-out is made, the Act could be brought before the House to remedy some of its shortcomings.
Over the years members of the New Democratic Party have suggested four or Five policy changes with respect to the Act. If we are unable to get an agricultural income security program or a grain producers' income insurance plan, we will not be able to look at it on a total basis as far as the Prairies are concerned. The Act should be changed so that it will be more effective in the future.
I know many government Members share our concerns, because when the House was debating the Act last year they

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act mentioned approaches which are similar to those which I will suggest today.
First, we believe that the plan should be more producer-specific. There should be a factor which allows a better definition of individual problems. For example, many of the farmers who are going under today are good farmers, but because they are beginning their farms, because of their debt load and because of high interest rates they are unable to meet their payments and continue having a good cash flow. A guaranteed cash flow would be worthwhile to them. However, we are not able to target money for that group. In our wisdom, if we looked at it we might decide that that is not an area where our concern should be targeted.
Second, we believe that the pay-out should be on a regional basis. I think there are very good examples for this which the Government has made some movement toward alleviating. For example, with respect to the western drought, and specifically the drought in southern Saskatchewan, if the rest of the provinces had a good crop and the prices were fairly high, southern Saskatchewan would not be able to get any money from the fund. Therefore we believe that we should be able to make those payments on a regional basis.
Another example would be the frost which on occasion has devastated crops in the Peace River area. Northeast Saskatchewan has had a considerable amount of flood damage in the past few years. Again, that area could have been targeted as a region which should have received money. If the majority of regions in the Praries have a good crop, there is no reason that a region which is hit by poor weather and therefore has a poor crop should not be able to get funds from the plan. That is why the plan is there.
Third, we believe that the plan should be more grain-specific. It should be grain specific because more and more of the farm population are specializing. Most of their crop will be peas, lentils or canola, barley or flax. Most have established some kind of rotation which is better for the land, but we still have those people who specialize in one or two grains. What happens if one crop fails? Maybe only one farmer in ten is affected by that failure, but if all of his land is in canola and there is no crop or the bottom drops out of the market, he is affected. Should he not have more of a call on stabilization in those kinds of circumstances? We think we should look at that.
The plan should be more oriented to the cost of production. That has been talked about on all sides of the House and there is a provision in the present formula, but we still have to recognize that at present the pay-out of stabilization payments is related more to cash income than the cost of production.
There is no real provision for labour, management or cost of investment, or even poor delivery opportunities. Perhaps that is one of the major factors. Right now we do not have too much trouble getting our grain to market because we have so little of it out in the west due to the drought. But there have been many years where we had poor delivery possibilities. In some cases we had two years of grain in the bin. Those kinds of
situations occur so the plan should be related more to farm income.
The Wheat Pool has made a suggestion which I think is worth looking at. They have suggested that farmers who grow their own feed grains should have an opportunity to pay the levy on that grain so that if they have a poor crop they will qualify for stabilization payments. It might be a little difficult to establish but it would be fair and worthwhile for those farmers who raise their own cattle and hog feed.
I am glad to say that this particular amendment takes care of one more shortcoming existing in the Act, the fact that farmers might have to wait for two or three months after the crop year before they got payment. This amendment makes it possible for the Minister to take action quickly when he knows there will be a pay-out and has some idea of the amount. I congratulate the Minister for that. The first step in this direction was taken last year by the Official Opposition and the New Democrats when we tried to have this amendment put in the Bill, but it was not accepted by the Government. So I congratulate the Minister on getting it done now. It is a short and quick method of getting the money out if it is available.
Those are my comments, Mr. Speaker. I just want to say that we hope we can get this Bill through the next two stages this afternoon and the Government can then start working on establishing a formula to get money to the farmers by spring seeding.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Very well. The Hon. Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, I declined to utilize my opportunity earlier today to respond to some of the very legitimate questions raised by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) in order to allow the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) an opportunity to commence his remarks before the one o'clock break. On reflection, I am pleased I did so because many of the questions raised by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry were also raised by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert. I indicated in a conversation I had with the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry that I would utilize this opportunity to respond to his questions. I appreciate the offer because I think there is an understanding that this legislation can be moved through all stages of the House today. I believe it requires an
February 15, 1985

amendment to the motion because the motion refers the Bill to the standing committee. Therefore, I have forwarded a motion to the Chair and I hope the Chair finds it in order so we can proceed with this Bill in all stages today. If that is the case, then we will not take very much of the time of the House. I feel somewhat guilty in taking the time I am going to take at the moment, but I do feel a responsibility to respond to some of the very legitimate questions raised.
Both Members raised the question whether or not it would be the position of this Government to open up the Bill for further study at a later date. I can give them that assurance. Indeed, if we had more time we would be quite prepared to open up the Bill for study and the amendment we brought forward today would be the result of those studies which could have taken place. But as both Hon. Members know, and as we have been cautioned by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry, time is short. We recognized that fact and that is the prime reason we brought the Bill forward, simply to allow an interim payment to be made as soon as possible.
My colleague, the Minister of State responsible for the Wheat Board (Mr. Mayer), has said publicly in the past that there are other matters we will want to consider. Indeed, some of these matters were flagged for us and raised in the speech of the Hon. Member for Prince Albert. We recognize there is a need. There have been requests for regional payments and we think it is a legitimate area to be looked at.
As well, the question of producer-specific has been raised before, perhaps by the Hon. Member, certainly by other grain farmers in western Canada, and we think it may indeed have some merit. I just want to acknowledge those as legitimate concerns which we share. If we had additional time we would study these matters which the Hon. Member raises.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry raised questions about damage to grain crops in western Canada which may be caused by pest infiltration in 1985. Some people may take that subject lightly. Those of us who have a better understanding of what this means in terms of crop and dollar losses to western farmers do not take the subject of grasshoppers lightly. I can assure Hon. Members that we are very concerned about it for a couple of reasons. One is that there are some early indications of a possibility of a larger infestation of grasshoppers in the crop year of 1985 than in that of last year. It will, of course, depend on weather conditions. If we happen to have an early and dry spring and a dry growing season, larger infestations of grasshoppers will be encouraged.
We are looking at this very closely. We are working closely with the provincial Governments. We have formed a federal-provincial committee of research scientists across western Canada. They are putting together a system to give a weekly update on the situation. Farmers in western Canada will have a contact point where they can obtain the latest update on grasshopper numbers. In Canada we have 10 licensed effective chemicals which can be used. We are watching the situation
Western Grain Stabilization Act very closely. We hope that the early indicators will not materialize.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry raised some questions which I do not think are legitimate. He asked why the subject of agriculture is not front row and centre at the First Ministers' conference which is about to conclude in Regina. A First Ministers' conference has not been held in this country since 1982. The main focus of the conference is the financial climate and economy of the country as well as interest rates and job creation. The problems in the agricultural industry and the importance of the industry in terms of the general economy and of job creation have been raised, as we would expect they would be, by provincial Premiers attending the meeting. To a large extent the agricultural industry depends on the general state of the economy.
There was some complaint that agriculture was only mentioned once in the Throne Speech. It was not a shopping basket approach. There were two very definite and strong commitments by the Government to the agricultural industry in the Throne Speech. The Government is fulfilling the commitments it made to the agricultural industry during the campaign in a very rapid fashion.
There have been concerns about what may happen to the Canadian farm economy as a result of certain actions which may or may not be taken by the U.S. Government through its farm Bill. Due to my responsibilities, I feel I should be the first to indicate that that matter concerns me very much. I doubt very much whether the U.S. Government will be able to carry out some of the indications which are flowing out of that country. There are large stockpiles of commodities in the U.S. If the financial support now in place is withdrawn, it will create very severe ramifications in the international marketplace. It is obvious that will have detrimental effects on the Canadian agricultural economy. I doubt very much whether some of these predictions will materialize to the extent that we think they might at the moment. There is no doubt, however, that they will follow more aggressive export sales promotion programs in the international market. We must be prepared to provide the same types of effective, aggressive and successful export programs to compete in the international market-place.
I can assure the Hon. Member that officials of my Department and officials of the U.S.D.A. are in contact with each other on almost a daily basis. I have had a number of conversations with U.S. Secretary John Block. My colleague, the Minister of International Trade (Mr. Kelleher), has had discussions with his counterpart in the U.S. We all know that our Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) has met the President of the United States and will meet him again next month. I am satisfied that these matters will be discussed on those forums. I hope that we can continue to compete on a fair and equitable basis in the international market.
I have perhaps not addressed all of the issues, Mr. Speaker. I am as anxious as anyone else to utilize the time of the House to the greatest advantage. I hope that we have the support of Hon. Members to move this Bill through the House. If there is a technical problem, I hope the motion which I have forwarded

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act to the Chair will be sufficient to allow us to pass this Bill through all stages in order to utilize the earliest opportunity to provide an interim payment to western farmers. If that is the case, as I assume it is, I would like to express my appreciation for the co-operation we have received from all quarters of the House on this legislation.
Mir. Deputy Speaker: I understand that the House agrees with the suggestion of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) that this Bill be referred to Committee of the Whole instead of the Standing Committee on Agriculture. Is that correct?
Agreed.
