speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. House in Committee of the Whole on Bill C-29, an Act to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act. Shall Clause 1 carry?
On Clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, this is the time to direct questions to the Minister if we desire to have this particular clause explained. Since the Bill does not indicate a percentage, is it the Minister's intention to provide approximately 50 per cent of the estimated pay-out? I assume that some preliminary calculations have been made. Approximately what would be the expected pay-out?
Mr. Chairman, that is a very legitimate question. I am not in a position at the moment to give the Hon. Member a definite answer.
Give us a guess.

Thank you for the invitation. I can make a guess. The safeguard is so that we will obtain as much information as possible. To avoid risking making an overpayment, we will take that information back to Cabinet where the actual assessment and decision will be made. We are told that we will be supplied with a fair amount of information which should be sufficiently reliable to make an intelligent decision, so we can make a reasonable payment but with the assurance that it would not potentially be an overpayment.

Would the Minister state whether the advisory board to the stabilization group would be consulted to determine the size of the pay-out? I recognize that the Act is not written in quite the same way as the Wheat Board Act, according to which the Wheat Board itself makes a recommendation to the Minister. The Minister takes this recommendation to Cabinet and with Cabinet approval the Government then accepts responsibility in the event that the initial pay-out for grains is too high.
I do not believe there is any such guarantee in this legislation. Will the advisory committee be utilized? Are there any guarantees against bad guesses so that the fund itself will not bear the burden of a bad guess? How is that approached?

Mr. Chairman, I expect that the advisory committee would indeed be the likely body with which consultations would take place. Indeed, it is there for a variety of reasons and should be very capable of advising the Minister as to what appropriate action could be taken. I would expect that it would be one of many groups that would be consulted. It would have an opportunity to give its input.
It is difficult to come up with an appropriate mechanism that would allow for an appropriate payment and, second, to be required to provide a safeguard whereby an overpayment would not take place.
In the absence of some suitable mechanism at the moment, we felt that the information that would come from the industry and would be available through statistics which are gathered by Agriculture Canada would be sufficient for the Cabinet to assume its responsibilities and make a reasonable and intelligent decision.

Mr. Chairman, does the Minister have a guideline at this point by which he could give us a range of the initial pay-out? Will it be 20 per cent, 50 per cent or 80 per cent of the final pay-out? Are you trying to give half of the pay-out before seeding and the rest when the final calculations are made, or, because of the circumstances this year and the great need for cash, are you looking at an 80 per cent pay-out?

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the legitimate reasons behind the Hon. Member's question. At this point I think it would be irresponsible for me to indicate what that particular target would be. There is a rather large amount of money in the fund. Second, there is a very tight cash situation in western Canada. If I mentioned a percentage, I am afraid that it would automatically become a minimum or benchmark. A benchmark for 1985 might not be appropriate for succeeding years.
I have some personal views about this, as does the Minister of State responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board. The final decision will be made by Cabinet but it has not been made yet.
I appreciate the information which the Hon. Member seeks and I wish I were in the position to provide it to him at the moment. However, I think it is somewhat premature for me to respond.
February 15, 1985

Mr. Chairman, I realize from his previous answers that the Minister is somewhat loth to make firm commitments. We have heard the Minister of State responsible for the Wheat Board say that it is his intention to have the cheques in the hands of the farmers before seeding. Since it is apparent that the Minister will not tell me a particular date by which he hopes to deliver the cheques, could he be somewhat circumspect and state when he thinks we will start seeding this year?
Mr. Chairman, I think there might be more of a degree of accuracy if the Hon. Member suggested to me the exact seeding date in all regions of western Canada.

Mr. Chairman, my question may also concern other clauses. The Minister will remember that many of us in the Opposition last year accused the previous Government of juggling the formula to fit the amount it decided to pay. Is there a specific formula or does one have to be calculated for each payment?

Mr. Chairman, I do not have the exact formula with me. I made reference to it in general terms in my speech. It is my understanding that the formula is in place. I do not think there is any juggling or any intention to juggle a formula in future years unless the recommendations flow from the western grain farmers and those recommendations have a great deal of merit and legitimacy.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister can correct me if I am wrong, but if my memory serves me rightly the income is calculated on the previous three crop years. If income is below 90 per cent of that three-year average in the current crop year, that figure is the payment. Does the Minister have the figures for the average income for the previous three crop years and what would be the projected income for the current crop year?
Mr. Chairman, I might have that information if I have a little more time to go through my notes. I will be happy to share that information with the Hon. Member if I can find it and it is here.
Agreed, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, my question follows from one asked by a Member from the NDP, namely that we have promised a pay-out before seeding. Sometimes in southern Alberta when people are seeding they are still plowing snow in northern Alberta. When it is springtime in the Rockies, sometimes people are still cleaning snow off their sidewalks 100 miles east of the Rockies. Different crops require different seeding times. It is difficult to say that we will do it all before May 24. We used to take as a rule of thumb that we have to have our potatoes and our wheat in by May 24. The varieties of wheat have changed and the varieties of potatoes have changed and that rule of thumb is not applicable now, but there is a deadline.
Western Grain Stabilization Act
Let us try to get the pay-out ahead of any seeding, well ahead of time because it is not simply the buying of the seed or the fuel, et cetera; there is machine repair and lots of preparation. Farmers require that money very badly this year. Many of our farmers are living from hand to mouth at the present time. Many people think farmers are really well off but farmers are going through a difficult and critical time in their history. We should make an effort to keep all of our good farmers. The ones having difficulties are mostly the young ones. Let us keep our good young farmers on the land. They will be essential to Canada, especially in the future.
Mr. Chairman, I want to place on the record that I never argue with representations made by the Hon. Member for Bow River.

I want to come back to the calculations again, Mr. Chairman. I understand the regulations are viewed with the cost production factor in the formula. They have been changed or they were changed in the last calculations that were done in June, or after June.
Would it be possible for the Minister to provide us with the formula and the regulations by which the cost of production is reached so we can have some insight into the process by which the Government is going to reach that level or the level that will be decided upon?

Mr. Chairman, I do not think I have any objection to that at all when I have the information available to me. There was some reference in an earlier question to the fact that the formula was based on the net cash flow for the previous three years. The information I have is that through stabilization payments they protect the net cash flow from the sale of seven major grains in western Canada-and we know what grains they are-from falling below the average net cash flow for the immediate preceding five-year period.
Do you have those Figures?

Mr. Chairman, we have heard some questions now about the pay-out side. I would like to ask the Minister some questions relating to the input side. My own information indicates that at the end of 1983 there was about $884 million in the Western Grain Stabilization Fund. This last year there was a pay-out somewhere in excess of $223 million which would bring the fund to the level of less than $600 million. The normal levies on federal participation and producer participation add another $130 million a year. In the Minister's opening statement, he indicated that he felt that the total pay-out by July could amount to some $800 million. I believe that was the figure he was using. In any event, it was pretty close to that.
Would the Minister tell us what the current state of the fund is? What would be the levies provided to the producers and what would be the federal contribution to that? What would be the estimated state of the fund at the end of the pay-out period next summer?

February 15, 1985
Western Grain Stabilization Act

Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether I can provide the Hon. Member with accurate information on that without some additional time. I believe the fund is somewhere in the neighbourhood of $900 million. I am not certain whether that $900 million was before the final payment of $123 million. The fund earns interest, of course. The information I have is that as of December 31, 1984, the balance was about $900 million. As a result of the drought on the Prairies last summer, producer marketings were expected to be down to six or seven million tonnes this crop year; thus a substantial western grain stabilization payment is expected to be triggered in the 1984-85 crop year under the total net cash flow calculation. Producers who had poor crops in 1984 require additional cash flows to enable them to seed their crops in the spring.
I do not believe the actual levy has changed where the contribution is 1.5 per cent of grain sales. If you look at the total picture, Mr. Chairman, the contribution is $1 for a producer and a $2 contribution by the federal Government.

Mr. Chairman, I recognize the Minister may have some problem providing the immediate figures. The point of the question concerns the state of the fund at the end of the pay-out period. It has an implication for the producers in terms of the amount of the levy. Again we are potentially caught in the squeeze between putting out on the one side and having to take on the other. Because of the substantially lower crop and sales expectation, the amount paid into the fund is on a smaller base and therefore may require a higher levy.
Part of the question is whether there would be consideration in the form of a moratorium on the level of payment under the Western Grain Stabilization Fund at this point in time so that we are not taking money out of one pocket and putting it into another in the same period, and therefore not giving that much benefit back to farmers at this time when the squeeze is on.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member raises a very legitimate question and one which has occupied a fair amount of discussion to this point in time. We recognize it is public knowledge that the fund is fairly sizeable. It is recognized that we have a responsibility because we have had numerous requests for us to make an interim payment by grain producers who have contributed to that fund. At the same time we recognize that we would want to be responsible in making that decision in such a way that a reasonable payment could be made to the farmers so as to put as much cash in their hands as early as possible and also to signal a greater degree of confidence. If cash was not placed in their hands, perhaps a greater measure of credit could be extended to them. We want to do it in a balanced way so that the actual fund is properly utilized, we do not run the risk of overpayment or of depleting the fund and we do not run the risk of having to increase levies.

Mr. Chairman, I have one final question in this respect. I have had some experience in the past with Finance Ministers who were very touchy about the question of
cash flows and relative levels of financing of different projects. I want to raise with the Minister what could be a difficult equation. Perhaps he will be faced with it. I should like to seek some assurances.
We in the House have heard that the Government is intending to bring forward a Budget in April or May, depending upon whose version of events one listens to. Let us say that the Budget will be brought forward this spring. We are now engaged in passing authority for interim payments. The final calculation will not take place until July 31. Therefore, we are in a position where, in a sense, the fiscal framework and allocations will be set in the Budget in the spring, before the calculation on the Western Grain Stabilization Fund has been set. There is a potential shortfall, certainly in terms of the actual federal contributions out of consolidated revenues.
Would the Minister assure us in terms of the budgetary process and the fiscal framework that sufficient funds will be set aside to ensure that full payments will be made, that the fund is considered stable, that it will maintain liquidity at the same time and that it will not affect the rate of levy to producers? The rate of levy to producers could be affected if the opposite happened; that is, if the Minister of Finance put forward a Budget, set the fiscal framework and then had the fund do its final calculations for July 31, realizing that higher levels of payment were required and therefore requiring a draw on more funds. This is a fairly important question, and we really need the assurance of the Minister in that respect.

Mr. Chairman, let me utilize this opportunity to correct the record. I think I referred to a two and one breakdown as far as contributions were concerned. I have been advised that this indeed was the case commencing January 1, 1984. Since then it has been 1.5 per cent for producers and the Government's contribution has been increased to 2.5 per cent.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry challenges us. Actually that is the challenge we face. There is somewhat of a risk if we want to provide an interim payment. I can assure him and other Hon. Members of the House that every precautionary step which can be taken will be taken to prevent us from getting into that situation. However, as a Government and because of our interest in the agricultural industry, if we find ourselves in a position where we have to accept our responsibilities as a result of some miscalculation, misjudg-ment or something of that nature, we will be as prepared to accept our responsibilities under those conditions, which we hope do not happen, as we are today.

Mr. Chairman, I want to ask a series of informational questions. If the Minister does not have the information, perhaps he could forward it to me or give it to the House in the future. That would be acceptable.
Could he tell us how much is in the fund right now, the balance? How much interest are we collecting on that fund from the Government?

The rate.
February 15, 1985

The rate of interest, yes. The levy was lowered for farmers about three years ago. I am just wondering about the process. Is it lowered by recommendation of the committee, or how is that decision reached? For instance, if we are getting short, is there a chance that it will be raised again? Finally, with the smaller crop this year, what is the expected amount of the levy pay-in?
I do not have all that information available to me at the moment, but I have no hesitation in providing it to the Hon. Member at a later date.

Clause agreed to.
Clause 2 and 3 agreed to.
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

The House resumed from Thursday, February 14, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bissonnette that Bill C-23, an Act to amend the Small Businesses Loans Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Regional Development.

Mr. Speaker, I am certainly glad to have an opportunity to speak on Bill C-23. Even though a 10-minute period for speeches is provided now, there are a number of things I want to say.
First, I support the Bill wholeheartedly because it will continue to be a boon to small-businessmen. Second, the situation faced by small-businessmen in Canada indicates that the Bill is badly needed.
We have heard some Hon. Members of the Liberal Party say that the Bill should be withdrawn, divided or thrown out. That would be a real slap in the face, to put it colloquially, for small-businessmen in Canada. They need this Bill. The fact that the money has already run out indicates that we need additional legislative authority to continue until March 31.
Every Member of the House who wants small business to progress should be in favour of moving this Bill forward as quickly as possible in line with full debate. If the Bill is delayed unduly, it means that some businessmen will not receive loans as there is no money left in the fund and it has to be supplemented by the $300 thousand which was mentioned by the Hon. Minister.
Some Hon. Members indicated that it was much better in 1981-82 and in 1983-84. I cannot see how this is so. Certainly it did a reasonably good job but there were defaults and deficiencies which should now be corrected. I believe this Bill will correct some of the things which have been discovered. The number of small businesses which went bankrupt in 1981 amounted to 8,005-8,005 businesses went out of business and into receivership or bankruptcy. In 1982, 10,765 businesses
Small Businesses Loans Act
went into bankruptcy. In 1983, there were 10,260. When Liberal Members say that this Act should be withdrawn, in light of that experience I do not think we would be assisting the small businessman.
No one on this side of the House thinks we should be giving hand-outs to small or large businesses, but there is a place for government money in order to keep businesses going such as seed money and other supplementary money. That enables a businessman to continue. Otherwise he may have gone into bankruptcy or receivership. During the last three or four years, that money often was not available because there were too many restrictions on getting the money.
Let us look at the small business bond, for example. When the Clark Government was in power, the small business bond was welcomed by the people with open arms. When the Liberal Government took over, people had to be in dire straits before they could get the money. That put the kibosh on that wonderful program.
There was a provision in the Act which said that loans could be made up to $500,000. I know a businessman who did not want to borrow any more than he had to. He borrowed $250,000. Due to rising prices and interest rates, which rose to the maximum during that period, he found he could not operate. When he returned for another loan, he was told, "We cannot do it". He was only permitted one loan. Even though he only borrowed half the amount, they would not loan the balance.
I went to the then Minister, the Hon. Allan MacEachen, and pointed that out. He said he would fix that. He agreed that the man should get the $500,000. I pointed out that he may want only another $100,000. He said he would look after this, but the departmental officials did not do that. I had the Minister's word verbally and by letter saying that he would arrange for the balance of that money, but he did not do it. What happened? Over 20 people lost their jobs. The business is now like a ghost. There are empty sheds.
I want to deal with one or two other points. Ten minutes is just not enough time. Are you signalling me that I have one minute remaining, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The Hon. Member has 20 minutes in which to speak.

You were pointing one finger and that made me nervous.
I want to deal with another item that was raised by a number of Liberal Members. I hope we can put their fears to rest. Some objected to the banks being responsible for any part of the losses. I do not follow that. All the losses would then be borne by the people, not by the banks. We would have a situation where the banks make the profit, maybe not as much as with normal loans because this has to be prime plus, and did all the arranging, and if there was any loss, the people of the country had to pay, that is, the government.

February 15, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
When the banks make a profit, they should be responsible for some of the loss. That is very reasonable. I would like to see it go beyond what this Bill says. It will not be changed in this fiscal year. After April 1,10 per cent of the losses will be paid by the banks. Why should that not be? They make the profit, why not be responsible for some of the loss? They made the contract. They might then make a more careful examination when making loans.
It is not right to say that people must pay the whole loss and the banks make all the profit. I do not go for that at all. I support this Bill which says the Government will pay 90 per cent and the banks 10 per cent. That is going the second mile, having the banks going for 10 per cent. I suppose the idea is to encourage the banks to make the loans, to look after needy cases. We will have to see how it works out. Certainly the other method did not work very well.
Let us look at the facts. In 1977, $96 million was lent and there were losses of $600,000. That was not too bad. However, let us look at 1984 when $900 million was lent and there was a loss of $43 million. The people had to pay that $43 million loss. Not only were the businesses lost, but the people lost $43 million and the banks lost nothing. They had their profit. I do not think that is a good record. No wonder the present Government says the banks should pay for part of the loss. That is right. I support it fully.
Another new feature in this Bill is that if the banks are going to make all the profit, they should pay a fee. If I were to go hunting and have the pleasure of hunting, I would have to pay for a licence. Nobody would give me the licence. I would pay for it. If I buy a car, I have to pay for a licence before I can operate it. Here the bank has the privilege of lending the money, with the Government picking up any losses and the bank paying absolutely nothing. We now say there will be a 1 per cent fee.
I suppose there is the danger of that fee being passed on to the borrower, but the Act will look after that. The banks cannot pass that 1 per cent fee on to the borrower. It will come out of the profits of the banks. It is about time the banks started paying some of these things instead of just taking all the time. I do not see anything wrong with the 1 per cent of the amount of the loan being charged, especially when it cannot be passed on. That will bring in revenue, which will compensate for some of the losses the people are taking. That is right and proper. Therefore, I support the Bill with regard to those points.
1 would now like to deal with the effect this will have on jobs. That is a very important item. Everything we do should consider those who are not receiving a pay cheque at the end of the week or the end of the month. The wife and children are under stress and strain because there is no pay cheque coming in. They may receive UIC, but that is only temporary. They cannot live a normal life. It is a tremendous help, but when that closes off, what do they have? All they are left with is welfare. That varies almost from municipality to municipality and certainly in every province. In some places it is reasonably good and in other places it is bad and the people barely exist.
An elderly citizen told me that for the last three days of the month he has soup and bread, and that sometimes he has to go without the soup and just have dry bread. In this country there should be a reasonable floor for our people. Whether you live in New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island, Quebec, Ontario, Alberta, British Columbia, or the Northwest Territories, you are a Canadian. The standard of living should at least be at a certain level. Whether you work or cannot work, whether you are on compensation of welfare, there should be a reasonable level, one that entitles you at least to live.
The truth is that most people want to work. They want to be independent. Many people would like to work but cannot find jobs, and this is particularly so for those in small communities who cannot commute to the cities in which some jobs are available. Therefore, we would like to see some jobs created through this Bill as well.
In my view, keeping our small businesses viable is one of the best ways of creating jobs in this country. I like the idea of small business. I like the idea of a proprietor, his wife and his family making the decisions. There are no boards of directors, large corporation lawyers or chartered accountants. It is only the man, his wife and his children who make the decisions, and if they make wrong decisions, they take the flak. Most times, their decisions are right because they are made in light of all the factors in that particular community.
One of the great highlights of free enterprise is that the proprietors make the decisions themselves rather than the Government and the chartered accountants. The man who has the money invested in that business makes his decisions, and he makes them in the best interests of his family and his community because he must live in the community and he must look after his family.
Every successful loan we make under this Act will provide jobs for more Canadians, including young people, women and men. There are small businesses in every community across the country right from the Atlantic to the Pacific, from Newfoundland to Victoria, from the 49th parallel to the Arctic Circle. There are people in those communities who need jobs. We are getting right down to the grass roots where the money is being utilized in the area in which the people live. There is a place for big businesses which can hire as many as 2,000 people. That is fine, but we still need the small businesses to look after employment in our communities throughout the country. Therefore, this Act is a job-creating Act.
A businessman who does not need the money will not borrow it. He will not pay prime plus 1 per cent when he does not need the money. If he has enough capital to keep going, then he keeps going. It is the man who is on the verge of failure or the man who wants to expand his successful business, provide more jobs, make more money and contribute to the nation who needs help.
I spoke to a man who lives in Black Diamond. He told me that he owned the empty lot that sat right beside the business he operates. He said, "I would like to build another building
February 15, 1985

on that lot. It would provide another eight or 10 jobs during construction and another three or four permanent jobs in this community. However, I am not going to do it". I asked him why this was so. He said, "Well, in the first place, no provision is made for a man of my capacity, a small businessman, to borrow money. I have to go to the bank and borrow at a high rate". He did not know about the Small Businesses Loans Act. It would have fit right into his plans. He went on to say, "Another reason for this is that I will work my fingers to the bone for my wife and my children but I will not work my fingers to the bone and then pay it all out in capital gains taxes when I pass away or retire".
Another thing we must do is to set the capital gains tax at a sensible level-nil. It is killing initiative today and is keeping businesses from expanding. It is stopping those who want to retire on the nest-egg they have built over the last 50 years from retiring because the Government will grab a percentage of half of it leaving them without enough to continue. Well, that is another Act, Mr. Speaker. However, it shows what small business can do if it is given the proper incentive.
That brings me to the last point I would like to make, Mr. Speaker, and that is that I think the Government has a responsibility to create a climate that will encourage people to invest. People say that Canadians have more money in the banks than any other people on the face of the earth. I do not know whether it is true or not, but if it is true or only partly true, then that money could be invested in ways that would pay bigger returns than bank interest rates or Canada savings bonds and people would be investing their money. When we invest money, we provide jobs. When we invest money, we increase the productivity of the country so that we can implement a good welfare program.
This tremendous economy of ours is all wrapped up together. We have a country with tremendous resources. We live in a country with tremendous people. All we need to do is put our resources and our people together, give them the wherewithal to convince the small businesses across this nation to invest, and we will make a big dent in the number of unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, I once again have the pleasure of rising to participate in debate on a Friday afternoon. I am pleased to do so when we are discussing a Bill that is as important to the small business community as this one.
I was quite taken aback and almost struck speechless by the opening comments of the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), an Hon. Member to whom I have listened on many occasions. In his opening elocution, he indicated that he was in favour of government doing something for the private sector on some occasions. That was such an incredible reversal and radical turnaround from the multitude of statements and comments I have heard the Hon. Member make over the years that I thought that it may have been caused by something he ate for lunch. Perhaps he had a conversion on the road to Tarsus. However, I could not believe my ears. He was actually saying that the Government itself, that nasty, horrible, evil
Small Businesses Loans Act
engine of destruction, would do something positive and constructive. I do not know whether that was a momentary lapse or whether he got carried away with his enthusiasm for supporting a mechanism of small businesses loans administration that was brought in and amended over the years by various Liberal Governments which saw the wisdom of having a program that would support small businesses in this country.
I was glad to see that by the end of his speech, he had reverted to form and was once again using his powers of erudition to flagellate government and extol the private sector.
I think the key question we are facing in this debate is whether or not the amendments proposed by the Government will assist small business. I have not heard anyone argue against helping small business. The key question in this regard is whether or not the specific amendments being discussed in the House provide for the necessary changes. Obviously the extension of the loan guarantees are an improvement and one to which I look forward. However, when I look at the other two components of the Bill, I find myself scratching my head.
I have heard that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) is off in Regina on his "grope and tell" session with the Premiers and they are all extolling the benefits of small business. However, we have in front of us an Act which, in very simple terms, will make it more difficult for small business to receive loans from the banks, chartered companies and trust companies. The question is, why is the Government doing that? Why would it deliberately go out of its way to make a change in the Act that will make it more difficult for small business to obtain loans? That opinion is held not only by members of the Opposition but has been widely expressed by members of the Federation of Small Business and by others in business. They simply say that by reducing the loan guarantee to 90 per cent and by charging a fee, the Bill makes it far less attractive for the lending institutions to provide the loans that are necessary. Surely that is a mystery. It is a conundrum. The Conservative Government, which believes, in the very depths of its theological soul, that private business is important, is putting additional barriers in the way of small business achieving its purpose. Frankly, I have no one who can give a plausible explanation for that other than the Hon. Member for Bow River who said that it is up to the banks to share in whatever losses may occur.
There may be some justice in the banks sharing the burden, but surely that is not the point of the Small Businesses Loans Act. The Act is to help small business invest, expand, and modernize to produce more and create more jobs. Contrary to every public statement, when it comes down to action, the Conservative Government is more dominated by a cost-cutting chartered accountant's view of the world than it is by a growth philosophy which would give small business a change. It only makes sense. If the Government is going to make it available to the banks at prime rate-and that would be the result of charging the 1 per cent user fee-then the banks will not give that kind of privileged opportunity to small business. The

February 15, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
banks will not give small business the advantage which was previously offered by the Act.
It is interesting that John Bulloch and Members of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business are saying that if the user fee is going to be charged, then it could be passed on to the borrower. That is a possibility which the Government should have examined. A strange mentality has taken hold of the Government. It must show a better balance on its own accounting sheets, as opposed to the larger question of national accounts, in terms of the over-all economic performance which involves jobs, growth, expansion and development. It is the primary responsibility of every Government to measure the economy by the total number of indicators and not only use what shows up in the calculations of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It is that curious finance mentality that the Government somehow thinks it is doing something useful if it shows that it has reduced the costs on the outlays when the Estimates are tabled. It does not matter that it will reduce small business growth, expansion and job creation. That does not seem to be important. What is important to the Government is an impression that somehow it has taken action and reduced deficits or cut back on the Estimates. It does not matter what damage it has done, what negative impact it has created, or the fact that growth has been retarded. That is a very dangerous precedent. It is a very serious problem, because if that is the mentality which drives and motivates members of the Ministry-and I am not talking about the back-benchers because they have said that they believe in small business-we are going to have a very difficult time over the next four years until a new Government assumes power. That Government will have a more positive point of view. This Government is putting anchors on the legs and wheels of small business.
I would like to talk about some interesting comparisons which have been made between small business growth in the United States and Canada. Several surveys and studies were done by the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion a year ago which indicated that Canada has approximately the same rate of small business creation as does the United States. However, there is one very major difference. In the United States, when a small business reaches a certain level of development, it has a much easier time becoming a medium or a large business. Small businesses in the United States have a take-off point. They are able to expand their markets, activities and, in particular, they are able to provide more jobs. In Canada, small business hits a dead zone. Canada has a much lower rate of small business upgrading, improving and expanding. Canadian small businesses tend to hit a level whereby they are no longer able to expand their activities. If we asked why, it comes down to the greater difficulty small business in Canada has in achieving venture capital for expansion and development. Canada has a more rigid financial market and less flexibility in the operation of capital markets as they apply to small business.
That is particularly true in western Canada which does not have many large corporations. I would say it is also shared in the Atlantic provinces. Small business forms the business
community there and it is what drives the economy in the West.
A recent survey was done by the Canadian Federation of Independent Business in the western region, and the major complaint of small business was the reduction in the financial system, especially with respect to the chartered banks. I have argued previously in the House that one of the most important initiatives we could take is a form of deregulation of the financial institutions to provide more opportunity for the caisses populates, credit unions and the smaller financial institutions which are locally based to expand their lending power and capacity. For example, small business in western Canada has indicated that the chartered bank system, with its rigid insistence on high levels of collateral, has become a frustration and a deterrent to small business development. There is a very clear and compelling argument that we must reorganize our financial system to allow for a much broader and more flexible flow of capital into small business for a wide variety of purposes. It is also important in the range of financial instruments which are offered by federal and provincial Governments.
A major problem-and it is a complaint which has been registered in previous lending practices, and particularly now under the new program of the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion-is that the service sector is totally ignored. The Economic Council of Canada in its 1984 report entitled Western Transition, indicated that one of the potential areas of real growth in the West was in the service sector. Yet that sector finds it far more difficult to receive financial backing and support from the Department of Regional Industrial Expansion, the IRDP, the FBDB, and other institutions which provide financial assistance. It is clearly the time for a major reform of both the private financial institutions and the federal and provincial lending institutions to deregulate, expand and make more flexible their offerings.
Over the past five or six months we have seen several actions which have contradicted that approach. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) radically changed IRDP. That is the major grant program for business. He has basically wiped out the opportunity for small business to get loans because the tier 1 allocation was removed. All small businesses in the major cities of Canada as well as in many other areas, were wiped out. Assistance is no longer available for expansion, modernization or renovation. Federal assistance to tourism has been removed. Tourism is a major service sector which provides incredibly labour-intensive job activity. The federal Government has withdrawn from that area. In that one act, the Government, which says it believes in small business, has eliminated a major area of support to small business. The Government will not tell us the reason and we are now seeing a major disparity between promises and action.
In addition, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion brought in the Investment Canada Bill. That Bill established thresholds, and the Government put the small business community into a real danger of being taken over by foreign investors. You do not have to take my word for it. Two days
February IS, 1985

ago we had the Conference Board of Canada, which represents the business community, saying the very same thing in committee. The question was asked: Do the present screening requirements under Investment Canada represent a threat to small business in the form of takeovers? They said, yes, and it should be amended to change that. The same Minister has, in his Investment Canada Bill, a further barrier to the expansion and development of small business. Now we have these amendments by the same Minister to the Small Businesses Loans Act which again puts up barriers. If you go back to the biblical injunction of being known by your actions, not by your words, then we have to say that this Government, because of its actions, clearly does not believe it should be giving assistance to small business. Never mind the rhetoric, the Fine speeches, look at the actions. It has eliminated IRDP loans and assistance for small businesses on tier one. It has eliminated grants for tourism. It has changed the Investment Canada procedures so that small businesses are now threatened by takeovers without screening or review. Then we have the imposition, under this Act, of user-fee requirements and a change in the loan guarantee provision, which means that private lenders will find it more difficult to give loans to small business. Logic and argument indicate we can only conclude that this is a Government which thinks that by smoke-screening, public relations, fine rhetoric and the spinning of homey phrases it can convince people of one thing, but the harsh reality as indicated by its actions in this House is that the Government is not a friend of small business. Certainly the Minister is not because every single thing he has done has worked against their interests.
I think this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, we have come to a very profound realization. The Conservative Government and the platforms upon which the Conservatives built, and the thousands of chamber of commerce speeches they have made, cannot be trusted. The Government does not live up to its promises. Furthermore, the small business community is being hoodwinked. In fact, what is far more dominant is this mythology and mentality that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Finance are showing neater calculations on their cost accounting sheets. That is what their objective is, not to create growth, opportunity or development.
The Hon. Member for Bow River asks why several Members of Parliament are saying that the Bill should be withdrawn. The reason is that it does not do what it should do, that is, to provide assistance and encouragement to our small business community to expand and provide job creation. It is bad legislation. Surely the Conservative back-benchers at their next caucus meeting should take the Minister off into a corner and whisper some words of wisdom in his ear. Not that he is going to listen very much. They should tell him that they are getting tired of this business. They are the ones who are exposed. They are making speeches in favour of small business, but they are going to be exposed as hypocrites because their Government is betraying them. Every single thing they do
Small Businesses Loans Act
works in contradiction to the interests of the small business community.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member can check Beauchesne, and in the meantime I will finish my speech.
Whether it is hypocritical or not, the fact remains that Conservative Members of Parliament are in danger of having their intentions subjected to some degree of skepticism because I believe their Government is betraying them. I say that with all my sympathy and with the intent to provide constructive encouragement and advice. They should change that Bill because no one in the small business community is going to thank them for having supported legislation which works against what they are trying to achieve. That is the hard reality they will have to face. All the brave promises that were made before September 4 are now being dashed to dust in the ground. This is a Government of big business, and that is the hard reality. All this consultation has not taken into account what the small business community is really saying. If this is a Government which really believed in consultation and in following advice, then why does it not change the Bill as small business has asked them to do? It is very simple. They said the user-fee will have a very serious deterrent effect on the provision of loans.
All we in opposition can do is to point out the fallacies and foibles and fumblings before us. We do not have the power to change them. That is why we are here this afternoon saying to those members of the government Party that they should take a hard look at this legislation and realize that they are doing no good. They are not providing any assistance or encouragement to small business. Therefore, the small business community will not be able to take advantage of opportunities to get the kind of capital it needs in order to expand and grow. That is really the message in this Bill. However, I hope that in this debate we will be able to ensure that by the time it gets to committee, the Minister will have come to his senses, will

February 15, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
listen to some of the good advice, and will make the amendments that are absolutely necessary to make this a good Bill.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Questions and comments?

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) did not want to mislead the House or anyone who may have been listening to his comments. He talked about the user-fee and putting impediments in the way of the small business development bond. He would recognize, and I am sure admit, that the small business development bond, when it was first introduced, was just that, a bond to help small business develop. When his Government got hold of it over the past four years, it became a rescue bond. It was no longer used for small business development, but, rather, as a bail-out bond, particularly over the last few years. It was a survival mechanism. The Government said it was not going to use it as a development bond any more. As a result, losses on the bonds became extremely high because we took away from the banks the discretionary use of the bond, as should be the case with good and normal planning practices in businesses.
What we are doing is putting some of the onus back on the banks. We are saying to them that they are going to lend the money and we are going to guarantee it, but there is a chance for a 10 per cent loss if they make a bad judgment. We no longer want to use this as a bail-out bond; we want to use it as a development bond. Surely the Hon. Member would understand that, would he not?

Mr. Speaker, let me provide the Hon. Member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) with two different kinds of answers, both of which I know he will find satisfactory. First, his description of the use of the Small Businesses Loans Act is not accurate.
If he goes back to the latest figures of the uses made of the money, he will find that in the year ending December 31, 1983, $70 million was used for fixed equipment, $408 million for moveable equipment, $76 million for improvement of premises, $35 million for construction of buildings, $85 million for purchase of buildings, and $14 million for the purchase of land. None of that is for bail-outs. It is for improvement, expansion, modernization and development. The basic purpose of the Small Businesses Loans Act is to give a small business entrepreneur, who sees an opportunity for a new business development, the necessary capital to make those choices. Those figures are in the small business loans report.
Mr. John Bulloch, who is known as a good friend of the Conservative Party and is the President of the Canadian Federation of Business, said that the Government would be crazy to make the banks pay the fee. We are trying to make that same point. He said that if we want to pass the user-fee on to the borrower we should examine that possibility. He said that taking the 1 per cent user-fee reduces the bank return to prime and, therefore, they will not make the loans. If the Government wants to recapture its fee and put it on the level
of the borrower, as Mr. Bulloch seems to be suggesting, it should look at that option. However, do not introduce an instrument into the Bill which will make it more difficult for a small business person to get a loan. The loan is the important thing. If the banks cannot get a return they will not provide the capital. They would prefer to make convertible loans or provide for a take-over or acquisition under the new Investment Canada Bill, or make some equally questionable use of the money.
It is the actual prescription of the Bill which is at fault. That is where the change should be made. That is why it is important to continue this debate. If Members on both sides of the House can be convinced of this by the time we get to committee, there may be a willingness to make that change.

Mr. Speaker, for the life of me I cannot understand why the Liberal Party is sticking up for the banks rather than for small businessmen. If the banks were doing their job a Bill such as this would not be necessary. They would be lending the money to worth-while small businesses. In this Bill we are telling the banks that we will pick up 90 per cent of the losses and that they can have all the profit and pay nothing. I do not think the banks are such poor corporate citizens that they will not make loans. It is in their interest to make loans. They will make the profit, not the Government. The Government will take up 90 per cent of the loss. The Government is the people. Surely a bank will not refuse to lend money for a sound investment because it will have to pay a 1 per cent fee. If banks are that bad, we should change the Bank Act. Part of the business of banks is to provide capital for business. This Act is a supplement. Surely they can pay 1 per cent on the loans when they are making prime plus 1 per cent.
I do not think the Hon. Member will get much support from businessmen in small towns by making such statements as he has here. You will find that the banks will be anxious to lend money. If I was in the business and could make 12.1 per cent, I would gladly pay a fee of 1 per cent. That would be wonderful. I might as well go into that kind of business. I disagree entirely.
The only parliamentary response that I cam make to the Hon. Member's suggestion that the Government is betraying the small businessman is to say, baloney. Small businessmen elected 211 Members on this side because they lost faith in what the Liberals were doing. They have confidence in the Government. We are building a climate in which they can invest their money and make a dollar. I will stand anywhere and support this Bill. The people are supporting it too. If the Liberal Party is trying to build up from the grass roots, it had better get some policies that appeal to the common people rather than only to the bankers.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, we have just now seen another prime example of Tory delusion. They love to use these words of rhetoric. They love to say that they believe in all these fine upstanding things. However, we are talking about action. I
February 15, 1985

suggest that the Hon. Member for Bow River read his own legislation. He should look at what the Government has proposed. He says that it is what the people want. I would suggest that he go back to his office and read the report of statements by the Canadian Federation of Small Business. It is opposed to that position in the Bill. John Bulloch, the President of the Federation, says that the banks, which have a number of competing demands upon their capital, need an incentive because small business does not offer the same degree of security.
The Hon. Member was obviously not paying much attention to my speech, although he should have been. I said that if the Government wants to be bold, it should introduce major programs to deregulate the financial system. It should give a lot more opportunity and flexibility because the chartered banks do have too much power. I have been arguing that for two years. I was the person who deregulated the airlines, which brought a lot more competition to that industry. I believe in that.
Do not tell me that this Bill will somehow help the small business community. It simply means that it will not have the necessary capital. If you are simply waiting for a major reform of the banking system, that is fine, but do not put a handicap in the way of small business in the meantime. That is exactly what the Government is doing. I suggest that before speaking, Hon. Members should read their own legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak in support of this Bill because, although it is not perfect, I think it is better to pass it and get on to other legislation. The objections which I have heard do not carry much weight in light of recent years. I will explain that point further. I would like to make a couple of other points first.
I take it that this Bill is being slightly updated to take inflation into account. The total insurable amount is being raised by $300 million, which I hope will make it more widely used. It probably just keeps up with inflation. The maximum size of a business to be considered a small business is raised from $1.5 million to $2 million. That again is to keep up with inflation. It is a necessary housekeeping amendment.
The extension of the length of loans to five years will give some people a better opportunity to plan than when decisions must be made in a one-year period. The issue of the user-fee and the 90 per cent insurance by the Government with 10 per cent left to the banks has caused a great deal of heat on the part of the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy), who got so heated up he just evaporated. I can understand his heat because the Government which he represented in past years followed a different policy. Its policy was to give as much as possible to the banks. The banks would then say that they would treat the public well with that money because they are so kind. That did not work. The banks have been shipping their money out of the country by the billions of dollars. They have been taking the largesse given to them by the previous Liberal Governments through the tax system and sending it anywhere but Canada. This money has been used by
Small Businesses Loans Act
them to finance companies like Cadillac-Fairview and Trisac that are now shipping their fortunes to the United States.
The legislation which has provided the banks with 100 per cent insurance and a free agency at the expense of the Government has not helped small business or job creation in Canada. All the benefits have gone to the banks themselves, and small businesses in Spadina have complained that this legislation has not allowed them to get loans from the banks.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry suggests that small businessmen will not be able to get loans from the banks if these changes are made. I suggest that there is no difference because it is only people who have changed sides of the House. The banks' performance will likely be no worse under this legislation than it was under the previous legislation. It will be interesting to see the results because I believe the user-fee is worth trying as an experiment. I suggest it is proper to call it a user-fee by the banks rather than by small business people. It is irrelevant whether the banks will pass it on to the borrower since they have already been doing so with the blessing of both this Government and the previous Government by jacking the rates up as high as the market would bear with absolutely no relation to cost.
The banks do not provide loans on the basis of cost; they do so on the basis of how much the market can bear. Therefore, I suggest that this legislation will not make any difference to the prime rate of interest, which it does not affect at all, or to the availability of loans. While it is suggested that it may increase the loans, the amount of money insurable for loans may increase but it remains to be seen if that will increase the amount of loans that the banks make. The banks' record in this respect has been very poor in the past.
The small business sector makes up a substantial part of our economy and provides over 40 per cent of all business employment. It provides a quarter of the Gross National Product and is almost 100 per cent Canadian-owned. It deserves more attention from the banks than it gets, and the fact is that the banks cause the most problems for small business.
Those businessmen to whom I talk in Spadina tell me that high interest rates and the difficulty of getting a loan when they need it, even with high interest rates, are their main problems. The banks cannot be bothered with processing a loan to small businesses; they prefer to lend to the big corporations. That has not made Canada stronger.
Let me give an example. Approximately six years ago, MacMillan Bloedel took over a section of the Continental Can corrugated box operation where I used to work. It shut down the plant where I had worked for 18 years. Some workers had put 10, 20 and 30 years of their lives into that plant and now they are still walking the streets looking for work. That takeover by MacMillan Bloedel did not create jobs, it destroyed jobs. Eventually MacMillan Bloedel had its own financial crisis and was itself taken over. In other words, this is an example of how the bloating of companies as a result of loans from the big banks is not healthy for Canada. The

February 15, 1985
Small Businesses Loans Act
banking money would be far better directed to the small business community.
Why have past Governments favoured the banks in the tax system and disfavoured the manufacturers where many of the small businesses are to be found? It appears to me that the present Government will follow the same policy. Why must manufacturers pay more than a third of their profits in tax while the banks generally pay less than a quarter of their profits in tax? This is essentially making the small and big manufacturers subsidize the banks.
In fact, in 1982, a couple of banks made $200 million or $300 million each in profits but paid no tax as a result of the generous taxing arrangements of the Government. Not only did they pay no tax, they received $20 million or $30 million in tax rebates.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. The Hon. Member indicated at the beginning of his speech that he supported the passage of this Bill at second reading today. Would he consider sitting down, with no one else rising, so that this can happen?

Mr. Speaker, I am in favour of this Bill being passed so that we can move to other legislation. I will not raise objections to the Bill, but there are others who wish to speak on it after today. I do not intend to support a move to terminate debate on the Bill today. I do intend to make some points that must be made because it is not perfect.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Government House Leader)
speechtext: Let's do it in committee.

The point I am making is that the situation is like that of the Irishman who does not like to be kicked with his own boot. The manufacturers in my riding, particularly in the garment and printing industries, do not like their taxes being given to the banks from which they must borrow it back at extortionist rates of interest. The Bill fails to address that issue or even to provide that a certain proportion of the banks' profits be made available by law to small business. Therefore, it is a defective Bill.
Let us get it into committee.

Rather than delay it by objecting at this point, I simply want to put certain points on the record. I realize that Members opposite do not want to hear any objections because they favour the banks. However, I believe certain points must be made. The interest payments as a proportion of our economy have been growing like a cancer. During one 16-year period, interest rates grew from 6 per cent to 15 per cent of the Gross National Product. The previous Government refused to consider that problem, but it is one which the present Government should take seriously.
I support the passage of this Bill but I ask that the Government consider some of the effects which I have pointed out. I hope that it will be wiling to consider some amendments similar to what I have suggested when the Bill goes to committee.
We will.

I am glad there is some willingness to reconsider this Bill with regard to its defects. I hope Hon. Members intend to allow a full debate on the Bill during second reading, which is the only time when most Members can contribute on general questions of principle.
