Agreed.

The House resumed, from January 22, 1985, consideration of the motion of Mr. Penner:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of promoting Indian self-government by:
1.	Announcing support for an affirmative policy of constitutional recognition of aboriginal self-government;
2.	Pursuing actively, a bilateral process of discussion with representatives of first nations on such issues as self-government, natives claims and the elimination of the extinguishment policy; and
3.	Introducing legislation to recognize first nations self-government which should be developed by means of a joint process and utilization of the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to speak on the issue of Indian self-government. As the House will recall, on December 4 the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner) moved this motion in the House. It was discussed again on January 22, and it is a pleasure to continue the discussion today.
I should like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior for the dedication which he has shown in pursuit of the interests of the Indians of the country. Over the years I, too, have had the opportunity of working with native people on issues relating to their economic and social development, both in Alberta and in the Northwest Territories. This has provided me with an opportunity to understand their concerns and aspirations.
February 15, 1985

I now have the honour to represent the people of the Squamish Indian band in my riding of Capilano. Over the past months I have had the opportunity on a number of occasions to have discussions with their representatives on issues relating to economic development and Indian self-government as they would apply to that band. I am pleased to advise the House, as it may well know, that the Squamish Indian band is perhaps a model for Indian self-government. The people of that band have shown their ability and commitment to provide for economic betterment and to play an active role in national native politics. They are able to take control and encourage their members to attain economic self-sufficiency while retaining their cultural values and sense of identity.
Obviously things are not perfect and there is much to be done. However that band, like many other bands in the country, deserves increased recognition and responsibilities for its land and its future. I look forward over the coming months and years to discussions about the best way this can be accomplished, understanding that there is differentiation among native bands across the country and each may need to work toward self-government at a different rate and in a different way.
I should like to spend a few minutes today providing some of the context for Indian self-government and to talk a bit about some of the economic issues. Indian self-government, as I understand it, was intended, first, to correct historic wrongs perpetrated by past Governments against the aboriginal peoples of this land. Second, it was intended to help establish a new economic basis from which Indian people could develop in the future. The historical view of this land held by aboriginal peoples is that prior to European exploration and colonization Canada was inhabited by many different indigeneous peoples, organized into political entities and groupings based on common language, culture and history. The Royal Proclamation of 1763 confirmed this view with its reference to "the several nations or tribes of Indians with whom we are connected".
Over the years, however, differing views of history developed. Indian people saw treaties as reaffirmations of their sovereignty and rights or as agreements to allow settlement in certain areas. Non-Indians regarded treaties as an extinguishment of rights, as an acceptance of the supremacy of the Crown or as a gift of land so that Indians might have land of their own. In more recent years there has been a wider acceptance of the aboriginal acceptance of history. Partly it was as a result of court decisions such as that of the Supreme Court of Canada in Colder v. The Attorney General of British Columbia. This 1973 case involved a title claim by the Nishga to an area in northwestern British Columbia. A more recent decision, again in British Columbia, of the Supreme Court in Guerin v. The Queen pointed out the fiduciary duty of the Crown to Indian bands.
Our view of history has also changed as a result of the articulate arguments of aboriginal people on their position at many constitutional meetings and other forums over the last few years, and also as a result of the all-Party Special Com-
Indian Self-government
mittee on Indian Self-government, led by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior, which in its hearings and in its report set out the reasoning for the aboriginal position.
I think the views of Canadians on aboriginal issues are changing for other reasons as well. Past efforts, explicit or implicit, have failed to bring about assimilation. Native groups have continued traditional practices and take pride in their culture. I think we as Canadians now recognize that and are ready to show our full appreciation of it. Also it is very evident that the past approaches to economic development for our native people have failed quite miserably.
I should like to provide some background information on that. For instance, the statistics from 1981 and other recent sources point out the failure of past economic approaches. The educational levels of native peoples are much lower than those non-native. Fifteen per cent of the native population over 15 years of age have less than grade five education, compared with 5 per cent of the rest of the population. Fortunately there are signs of hope in this area. Only 3 per cent of young natives aged 15 to 29 have not gone past grade five, compared with 57 per cent of natives 65 years and older. Changes are taking place. Again I can point to the band in my own riding where there is an increased emphasis upon education and an increased awareness among the parents of the importance of education for young people. There is also a desire that they have some role in that educational process and that part of that process include consideration of their culture and their values.
The incomes of status Indians on reserves are just over half or 54 per cent of those of the non-native population. In 1980 the average income of natives on reserves was $7,100, compared with $13,100 for the non-native population. Incomes for native people as a whole are little better. They are two-thirds of the non-native average.
The employment rates of natives, particularly for those living on reserves, are much lower than for the rest of Canadians. In 1981, half the adult native population was in the labour force, compared with two-thirds of non-natives. For those on reserves, only 42 per cent of the men and 22 per cent of the women were employed.
We all know the circumstance with respect to housing. The housing of native people is often poor. I recall that being the case in some of the areas of Alberta where I worked and in Ontario as well. The 1981 census found that the proportion of homes needing major repair on Indian reserves was nearly one in four compared with one in fifteen for non-native homes. Half the homes on reserves lacked central heating, compared with 9 per cent of non-native homes. Bathrooms were lacking in 30 per cent of on-reserve housing, but in less than 1 per cent of non-native homes. One in three homes on reserves was crowded, compared with one in 43 non-native homes.
When we reflect upon those figures we see some of the difficult social conditions under which many native people on reserves live. They are conducive to some of the problems they experience. Changes in the economic prospects of aboriginal people will not come about easily. They will not come about as

February 15, 1985
Indian Self-government
mere hand-outs by federal or provincial Governments. They will not come about overnight, but I am pleased to say that steps are being taken now by the Government.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) has announced that he is exploring a means of introducing new funding arrangements for Indian bands and tribal councils. Such funding arrangements would enable the bands and councils to decide how best to meet their people's needs, to set their own priorities and to make their own policies within the limitations of current legislation. Thus it is hoped that changes in line with self-government can be implemented soon.
The need for other changes is fully recognized. We need to fund an improved community infrastructure, we need to end the duplication of programs on reserves which result in wasted dollars, and we need to examine the introduction of a system of direct transfer payments. This is now being examined.
As has been said before, we must find a way, in these times of restraint and fiscal responsibility, to provide a level of funding sufficient so that First Nation Governments can provide levels of service on a par with others in Canada, which will allow them to become healthy and productive communities. This can be done only when funds can be expended in accord with their own values and under their own control.
We know the priorities of this Government. The economic revitalization of this country is a major goal of this Government. We have heard what has gone on in Regina over the last two days and how we are looking toward a new harmonization of federal and provincial goals. This revitalization is clearly needed for our aboriginal people as well as for our other citizens. For this reason, the Speech from the Throne which opened this Parliament called on native peoples to be part of the process of building a national economic consensus.
Plans are well under way for the participation of native peoples in the national economic conference scheduled for March 1985. Of course, the next First Ministers' conference on aboriginal constitutional matters will take place in April, 1985.
There is much that will be happening in the future to further our concerns and initiative toward Indian self-government. Hon. Members may be assured that our Government is looking for new approaches to replace the policies which have failed in the past. We are talking to native people and we are seeking their views. We believe that in this spirit of reconciliation, the spirit of harmonization, we will be able to do better. The native people of this country can look forward to a better economic future, a future which takes fully into account their own aspirations.

Mr. Speaker, the motion before us is to study very thoroughly the question of Indian self-government. It tends to set out general approval for such a move. I was quite moved by the speech we just heard by the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) concerning the Government's intention to reconcile the Canadian people and the various competing interests. She
spoke very warmly of the harmonizing of this new approach that is being adopted by this new Government. Given the good feelings and indication from the government Member, now would be a very suitable time for us to send this particular motion to the Standing Committee on Indians Affairs to be acted upon. I will not hold up the House any further. I simply hope that we will pass this on to the appropriate committee at this time.

Mr. Speaker, as usual it is a pleasure to speak to the House on a Friday afternoon. People have completed their week's work and they are especially attentive to the thoughts that are expressed here. The topic today is one of interest to Members of the House, perhaps of more interest to us who have had the privilege of serving on the joint committee which examined the Canadian Constitution. There are many reasons for those of us who had that privilege why that experience will last in our memories for a long time. The work was important. It proceeded at a fairly rapid pace with a lot of long days and long hours.
Canadians probably remember the work of that committee in a way that is different from the work of all other House of Commons committees because the proceedings were televised. That is the only opportunity Canadians have ever had to watch a joint committee, House committee or Senate committee in action. Many of my constituents told me over the years that they would like to see that experience repeated because they found it educational. They learned a great deal. 1 spoke to many constituents who used to spend their weekends watching the reruns. Of the literally hundreds of witnesses and hundreds of briefs that we received, it was the native people who perhaps had the greatest impact on the Canadian psyche, both because of the quality of their presentations and, to some extent, the frequency of their presentations.
Those short three or four months back in 1980 and early 1981 accomplished a great deal in raising the awareness level of the average Canadian about native people in this country, what their strengths are and could be and what are some of the difficulties that they face. Those were the early days of the serious lobbying done on behalf of the Indian people for a concept that they referred to at that time as Indian selfgovernment.
As a member of the committee, I shared something with the other members of that committee in that we had a great deal of difficulty in understanding what that meant and what the repercussions would be for the Indian people and for the nation as a whole. It speaks to the level of understanding that developed in the committee members that that difficulty which existed for the committee members at the beginning has remained at the end. It was truly a reflection of the difficulty that Indian people were having themselves in understanding what the words meant and what the repercussions would be for them personally and for their place in Canadian society.
I stand here today in the early part of 1985 with the knowledge that the concept has been refined, developed and probably is becoming clearer to a great many Canadians, including the Indian people themselves. I also know that the
February 15, 1985

definition is not complete. It is not a fully defined concept. It is not one that would have instant universal recognition and agreement as to its meaning.
When I look at the motion which we are debating today I find there is a kind of intuitive positive reaction toward its wisdom and the fact that it is probably a good idea. That is the initial reaction. Then we must stand back from it and think it through a second time. We must wonder whether or not it really deals with the right set of words and with the right process. For instance, is a parliamentary standing committee the best body before which such a complex concept may be examined?
Changes in society that are of fundamental importance, and I think constitutional revision is always the kind of change that is of fundamental importance, should never be entered into lightly and should probably not be entered into quickly. Once something is placed in a constitution, then it is difficult to change, so it may be that the quicker it is done, the less likely we are to spot most if not all of the unintended consequences. I think it behooves us as elected Members to be very careful about movements we make in that regard. Any piece of legislation is serious and has repercussions. We should always be careful, but when we move into the constitutional area, we must be especially careful.
In early 1981, the constitutional committee reported back to Parliament. In its report to Parliament, it recommended major changes to the Canadian Constitution as it affected aboriginal peoples. Standing here today, I realize that there has not been sufficient time for all of those changes to work their magic, good or bad, on the situation. In other words, I do not think that Members of Parliament, the Canadian people or the Indian people really understand the long-range implications of that change in the constitutional position.
At the heart of this motion lies an effort to enshrine one more principle in the Canadian Constitution, the principle of Indian self-government. The motion leads us toward that. Yet nowhere do I see a very thorough analysis of what that right might do to the rights which were enshrined when we recently made those constitutional changes. We enshrined the concept of aboriginal rights.
Perhaps I could read into the record those parts of the Act affecting Indian people which came into effect when the Constitution Act was proclaimed in 1982. In section 25, we see that the following was the will of that Parliament and those bodies which signed that Constitution:
The guarantee in this Charter of certain rights and freedoms shall not be construed so as to abrogate or derogate from any aboriginal, treaty or other rights or freedoms that pertain to the aboriginal peoples of Canada including
(a)	any rights or freedoms that have been recognized by the Royal Proclamation of October 7, 1763; and
(b)	any rights or freedoms that may be acquired by the aboriginal peoples of
Canada by way of land claims settlement.
Indian Self-government
Section 35 goes on to say:
(1)	The existing aboriginal and treaty rights of the aboriginal peoples of Canada are hereby recognized and affirmed.
(2)	In this Act, "aboriginal peoples of Canada" includes the Indian, Inuit and Metis peoples of Canada.
We went further by requiring that a constitutional conference be held within one year. It was the wisdom of Parliament, acting on the advice of a special joint committee which had laboured long and hard and sometimes under very difficult circumstances, to arrive at sets of words and principles that would lock in place something that the aboriginal people indicated to us was important to them and that they wanted. It also set in place a process.
I would like to take a moment or two to examine the process that was set in place. The conference that was required was held in March 1983. It was a First Ministers' conference attended by the two levels of Government that are recognized in the Canadian Constitution, namely, the federal and the provincial. The subject matter was the rights of aboriginal peoples, and they were represented at the table. The federal Government, the provincial Governments and the aboriginal peoples reached some accord and, perhaps more significantly, one of the items on which they agreed was to have a minimum of two further constitutional meetings before April 1987 for the purposes of identifying and defining the rights of aboriginal peoples.
In March 1984, the first of those conferences was held. It was another First Ministers' conference on the rights of aboriginal peoples, and no agreement was reached at that conference last March. The conference dealt with four items: equality rights; aboriginal title and aboriginal rights treaties and treaty rights; land and resources; and aboriginal self-government.
The Hon. Member who moved the motion that is before us today asked us to pursue actively a bilateral process. I suppose those words really twigged me. Because of our desire in the early part of the 1980s to change the Constitution and to enhance the position of aboriginal people in our society, we said that some things were possible and other things must come about through proper process. We decided on the proper process at that time and it involved the federal Government, the provincial Governments and the aboriginal peoples. It was a tripartite process. That tripartite process in the early part of 1985 has not produced the kind of final results that we as members of that committee envisioned back in 1981-82. I do not think I can go the second step and conclude that it will not produce those results. In fact, I believe that it is the most likely kind of process to produce the kind of results that we will be able to support, believe in and make happen in a consensus fashion.
I see this matter as being analogous to so many things that we have in our society. When all of the bodies that are truly and significantly affected by an issue are given the time, the proper atmosphere and the meeting space, though the process is a little sloppy and a little long, it does tend to produce decisions that have a great many more positive aspects than

February 15, 1985
Indian Self-government
negative ones. It tends to produce the kinds of decisions that do not have unintended side-effects which we do not value and cannot support.
It is the notion of process with which I most violently disagree in the approach which was recommended to us by the Hon. Member who moved this motion. After the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) has travelled the country and met with aboriginal groups and when he goes to the conference table and represents the federal perspective, I think that by the time of the next conference there will be a better understanding. If the Government continues in a wide range of activities to act the way that it has, with the sense that this is a Confederation and that the consultation process is important and fundamental, then at the next conference on the issue which is of concern to us today there may be a change in attitude on the part of some of the provinces. That process may produce the kind of understanding which lies at the heart of positive and solid solutions.
For that reason I would urge Members not to be premature in starting a side process which would detract from the process which our best wisdom told us some time ago was the kind of process required to resolve the situation and advance the cause of aboriginal people. That is the goal. We want to improve the situation for aboriginal people in Canada. Most of us in the Chamber believe that the concept of self-government is at the heart of the solution. We might not all agree on exactly what that means, but we know that it is important for the people in local communities to have control over many aspects of their lives. When the provinces created municipalities, cities and so on, they gave democratic powers to people to elect representatives who would make the by-laws, to have their own police force, et cetera. The belief is that the people of the community know best how to run their community.
For decades aboriginal peoples have been denied that right. They were denied the right to vote for far too long. We are progressing to the point where it is essential to negotiate the concept of Indian self-government. I will tell Members that in those negotiations aboriginal people must be at the table, the federal Government must be at the table and the provinces must be at the table. If we are to change government and governmental arrangements in the country, all parties which are affected must be at the table. Then and only then will we obtain the correct solution, the most desirable solution and the solution which will endure and enable aboriginal people to prosper.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure to address this particular issue. As this is the first time I have addressed this House, I would like to begin by telling you a bit about myself.
I was born and grew up in Manitoba, which all Members know is the heart of this continent. My father was an immigrant who came to Canada in 1928 and established a farm. We are very proud of our achievements as farmers in Manitoba. My father achieved success at farming through hard work.
It has always been the philosophy of our family that if one wants to succeed, one needs dedication and hard work. I suppose that is how I got here.
Hear, hear!

My interest in this subject stems from the fact that I was always involved in agriculture and that I developed a business at one time which exported Canadian agricultural products around the world, particularly purebred hogs and cattle. I entered the field of exporting products to Mexico, which also has many natives who have problems. Mexico does not have a welfare system, or very many social assistance programs, but it has a good number of people who are at a poverty level far lower than what is known to people in Canada. However, Mexico managed to devise some programs which were absolutely fundamental in improving the standard of living for some tribes of Indians who live in the remote regions. They sat and collectively put together economic units with the help of the Government so that food and shelter would be provided. I was amazed at how effective that process was.
Over the course of the years, the Canadian Government has tried, but in many instances failed, to achieve the things it wanted because it did not consult with the Indians of Canada. In the last few months I visited all the communities in my riding, as well as many others, with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie). All too often people told us that it was always the Canadian Government people who told them what they were going to get but they had never been consulted. I guess that has been the case over the last 100, 200 or 300 years. Not being there when it first began, I think the time has come when we have to sit, listen and discuss these issues with these people. They are just as important a part of our community and our country as any one of us. We should never forget that.
I think the meaning of the words self-determination and self-government have become very confusing to many people in this country. Many, many people will ask if this means we are going to give the Indians their own country. Are we going to have borders and they will have their own passports? People really do not understand what we are trying to achieve or what the natives of this country would like. I think it is up to us as Canadians to show them that what we are trying to do with the Indian reserves is to give them the same things we have in our municipalities. They should have the right, in a democratic way, to decide where they would like to put a ditch or new roads or what kind of development they want. Those things which we take for granted every day are the things that have been denied many of these individuals.
It is not a perfect world, Mr. Speaker. As these people come to my office, as I am sure they do to your office, to talk about their concerns, they tell us that the welfare system is hurting their people. I am often amazed that when these individuals come in they say "my people". Do you ever go home and say
February 15, 1985

about your community, "these are my people"? I am sure the only people you say are your people are the ones in your own house, and beyond that you do not care. But when they come to my office, they describe their community as "my people". I think that is absolutely wonderful.

A point of order, Mr. Speaker. I am sure that the Hon. Member would not want to insinuate that other Hon. Members do not care for their constituents. We often refer to them as "my people", and I am sure he would agree with that point.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: That is not a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I do not know what problems the Hon. Member has, but I would like to continue if I may.
I would like to advise all Members of this House that if they do have Indians and natives in their area, they should invite them over to their offices and visit their reserves. There is a message out there for them. We have to work together to bring the needs of this group of people to a satisfactory conclusion so that they have the honour and respect they deserve.
Over the years, Mr. Speaker, we have instigated different ways to help through legislation. Yet when you talk to the particular bands, you find that all too often they are totally frustrated with the system. They have no way of finding out things which will benefit them without having to engage consulting firms. Representatives of one individual band came to me just to build a basic elementary school or upgrade the one they had. They had to come to Ottawa at least six times over the course of a year and go to the regional office in Winnipeg about 20 times and almost beg on their knees to get some funding for a school, which we back home take for granted. I want everybody to think about that. If you had to do that in your community, I am sure you would take up arms, and I would not blame you. But we expect them to work under that system. The bureaucratic system we have developed for those bands to achieve some economy is the most frustrating thing they have to deal with every day of their lives. That is what we have to change. We have to bring about some real stability in this particular area which I think has been lacking for too long.
Consider the fact that many Indian bands have 90 per cent unemployment, Mr. Speaker. Put the other way, only 10 per cent have jobs. Realistically there may not always be an opportunity for those bands to obtain an economic base which would allow them to achieve 100 per cent employment. We cannot put a parts factory or a lumber yard in an area where natural resources do not exist. Their past livelihood revolving around hunting or trapping is no longer available because the animals no longer exist. There is no realistic form of economic growth we could even dream up. Those are the realities. How we are to help them achieve an economic base is going to take the collective wisdom of everyone in this House.
I have taken my job very seriously in this area, Mr. Speaker. I have taken seriously the approach that was set out by our Hon. Minister, who has worked at least 14 to 16 hours every
Indian Self-government
day to try to seek their guidance and consultation in trying to find a solution to some of these very serious problems. I believe the Minister's desire to make some significant changes during the mandate of this particular administration, and the one I will be a part of next time, is very honourable and the most dynamic piece of legislation to deal with the reserves which has ever come to Parliament. It is together with my friends in both Parties in opposition that we will work diligently to achieve this type of legislation. The most important point I would like to make is that we should consult with the individuals and their leaders from coast to coast so that their input is used to bring about policies which will help them in the future.
I do not know how much time I have left but I would like to indicate that the whole economy of Canada is a vital element in our attempts to carry out the many programs we would like to carry out in this Government. By getting our economy going we can obtain the funds we need to help these special interest groups. I do not see how we can continue to run a deficit, because the people we help will end up having to live with the deficit and find ways and means of paying it back. That is the situation we are in. Our desire is to bring Canada into the 21st century, to make it a dynamic and exciting place to live. But over the last four months I have sat here and listened to nothing but criticism from the opposition Parties. They never demonstrated a single way to stimulate the economy. The only way they want to stimulate the economy is to reach into someone else's pocket in some other country, bring some money in and keep it rolling at least temporarily.
That is what Mulroney wants to do.
What about low interest rates?

There they are, Mr. Speaker. They did not notice when interest rates came down from 22 per cent to 13 per cent. Not one of them was excited about that. But it went up one half of a per cent and they are all crying and gyrating around the House.
Not too long ago I heard some of my hon. colleagues in the New Democratic Party saying that their policy is to use Canadian funds which are invested in banks to develop the country. Every six months the Premier of Manitoba would whip over to Japan and pull in $70 million. Then he would whip back over to Switzerland and haul some more in. However, that is not their policy. It just did not make sense. On the one hand they believed in one thing and on the other hand they believed in another. They do not know what they believe in but they will criticize anything we do. Let us get together on a policy like the one we were discussing before to get the economy going. I was surprised to see that they supported it.
Those are my real concerns in this regard. This particular resolution was not even necessary because the things indicated in it are happening. We have a Minister who is determined to make the necessary changes. He is on the right track. He has the consultation attitude which we never had in the 22 years of Liberal rule. This Government gives everyone an opportunity

to discuss. I suppose that is a wonderment to the NDP, which also sat in opposition in the Liberal administration. The NDP must notice the difference with our open attitude.
I have enjoyed speaking in the House for the first time, Mr. Speaker. I have got the shakes out of my feet now so you will see me rising to speak more often. I look forward to debating many subjects in the coming months.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, that is a tough act to follow. I would like to take this opportunity to congratulate my colleague on his maiden speech in the House. It was delivered with eloquence and compassion on a subject which is obviously important to him and to his constituents. I recall his telling me a week ago about his trip to the North with the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Crombie) visiting Indian bands. I represent an urban riding in the City of Ottawa where there are no Indian bands and relatively few native people. In fact, the 100 or 200 who are there are probably employees of the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development. Despite that, I am glad to have an opportunity to take part in this debate on an important national issue.
The Hon. Member's motion says that the Government should consider the advisability of promoting Indian self-government. As the previous speaker made clear, that is one of the prime concerns of the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and of the Government.
An all-Party special committee of the House, chaired by the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner), examined the issue of Indian self-government some time ago. This committee was unique in that it included an ex-officio member from the Assembly of First Nations and two liaison members from other native organizations. The special committee played a very important role. It clearly articulated the concerns, needs and desires of Indian people for self-government. It raised the awareness of Candians about Indian seelf-government.
The committee travelled widely in Canada as well as in the United States. It heard the views and experiences of many groups and individuals. The special committee's report was tabled on November 3, 1983, less than a year after the creation of the committee. It contained 58 recommendations concerning Indian self-government on a broad range of matters, some of which I will mention.
First, the principle of the constitutional entrenchment of self-government by which the federal Government would seek to establish a new relationship with Indian First Nations and confirm that relationship by means of a constitutional \ amendment.
Second, legislation as an interim measure to provide for recognition of Indian First Nations as well as to accommodate
the full range of governmental arrangements sought by Indian First Nations.
Third, membership for Indian Governments and the process by which this would be determined.
Fourth, the federal responsibility for those people eligible for Indian programs but who are not members of Indian Governments, as well as responsibility to respect the rights and aspirations of all Indian people.
Fifth, the process for recognition of Indian First Nation Governments.
Sixth, the scope of powers for Indian Government, including legislative and policy making powers, control over territory and resources within Indian lands, with the exact scope of jurisdiction to be negotiated by individual Indian First Nations.
Economic foundations for Indian self-government were also included in the recommendations, including adequate land and resource base, settlement of claims and funding. Another recommendation was fiscal arrangements to support Indian First Nation Governments. Also included were lands and resources for Indian Governments, the extent of control, and the various means to achieve full control of Indian lands and resources. Another recommendation was the resolution of claims, including the principle for a new claims process. A further recommendation was the trust relationship between the federal Government and Indian First Nations and the need for it to be renewed and enhanced through constitutional amendment, legislation, and other means. One final recommendation that I will mention was the idea of trust accounts for Indian First Nations and the means by which they should be transferred from departmental authority. There were many other recommendations but those were the most important, Mr. Speaker.
A response to that special committee report was tabled on March 15, 1984. It responded only in a very general way to the recommendations. Moreover, the general framework legislation on self-government for Indian nations, which was proposed in the response and which was introduced in the final days of the previous Parliament, left many issues still not resolved to the satisfaction of Indian peoples.
Key issues surrounding the process of recognition or the type of powers for Indian Governments were not simply or directly handled. The economic foundation and lands and resources relating to self-government were not addressed comprehensively but were left for future work.
This piece of legislation has been harshly criticized by members of the previous Government who called it "an inadequate flawed Bill... totally unacceptable". There are many issues on self-government which need to be considered, Mr. Speaker, which were not fully dealt with in the previous response to the report of the special committee. These issues
